#6380. Kimchi Bolognese

I’ve always loved Italian American food. Maybe because Italian and Korean cooking have traits in common: Both are homey and resourceful, and grandmothers are revered for their signature dishes made without formal recipes. This recipe was one of the first Korean Italian fusion recipes I developed, and it makes use of my two favorite secret weapons: kimchi and fish sauce. The result is the Bolognese you know and love, but with a deep, tangy twist. Fish sauce in Italian cooking is not a new idea, actually—Romans have been using salted anchovies and garum, an ancient kind of fish sauce, for centuries. For an extra-special finish, I love garnishing this with baek (white) kimchi for acidity. But it’s optional, and regular kimchi (or no kimchi) works just fine, too.

Start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Stir in 1 medium-yellow onion, finely diced (about 1½ cups), 2 carrots, peeled and finely diced, and 3 stalks celery, finely diced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and the edges start to brown, about 4 minutes. Stir in 4 cloves garlic, minced, and a pinch of kosher salt and cook for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 cup chopped kimchi and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook until the kimchi pieces start to soften, about 3 minutes. Pour in ½ cup red wine, increase the heat, and simmer, stirring with a wooden spoon to dislodge any bits that have stuck to the bottom, until the wine has nearly disappeared, about 2 minutes.

Add the meat: Stir in 1 lb. ground beef, season with generous pinches of salt (at least ½ tsp.), and cook, breaking up the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.

Add the tomatoes: Pour one 28-oz. can whole San Marzano tomatoes in a bowl. Using clean hands, squish the tomatoes into small pieces. Pour the tomatoes into the pot and add 1 cup beef broth or water, ½ tsp. dried Italian seasoning or dried oregano, a pinch of salt, and a few grinds of freshly ground black pepper. Bring to a simmer and lower the heat to medium-low. Gently cook, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is just thick enough to stand up on a spoon, about 20 minutes. Stir in 2 Tbsp. fish sauce and taste, then add more salt or fish sauce if needed.

Cook the noodles and serve: In a pot of boiling salted water, cook 1 lb. spaghetti according to package instructions, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until al dente. Drain the noodles in a colander, then give the colander a shake to get rid of extra water. Divide the noodles among serving plates and spoon the Bolognese on top. Garnish with 1 cup chopped kimchi (white or regular; if using) and 2 Tbsp. chopped flat-leaf parsley and serve.

Do Ahead: Leftover Bolognese sauce (without the noodles) keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, or in the freezer for up to 2 months.

#6378. Anchovy-Garlic Pasta

Even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

#6377. Crêpes Suzette

Credit for inventing crêpes Suzette is claimed by French restaurateur Henri Charpentier, who in 1894, at age 14, while an assistant waiter, accidentally set a sauce aflame when serving dessert to the Prince of Wales. Once the fire subsided, the sauce was so delicious that the prince asked that the dish be named for a young girl in his entourage, Suzette.

Featured in “Blazin' Pancakes” by Mindy Fox in the January/February 2000 issue and  “Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?” by Ellery Weil.

Global recipes, tastes, and trends—straight to your inbox.

Delicate pancakes are layered in a sweet orange-butter sauce and then set aflame in this classic French dessert.

Credit for inventing crêpes Suzette is claimed by French restaurateur Henri Charpentier, who in 1894, at age 14, while an assistant waiter, accidentally set a sauce aflame when serving dessert to the Prince of Wales. Once the fire subsided, the sauce was so delicious that the prince asked that the dish be named for a young girl in his entourage, Suzette.

Featured in “Blazin' Pancakes” by Mindy Fox in the January/February 2000 issue and  “Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?” by Ellery Weil.

#6376. Dirty Martini Latkes

If your holiday spread always includes a plate of crispy latkes and a round of dirty martinis, these dirty martini latkes are probably your dream mash-up. This playful party app takes everything you love about the classic Hanukkah potato pancake and gives it a cocktail-inspired twist with buttery green olives, pimento peppers, and a tangy blue cheese and vermouth-spiked sour cream for dipping. The blue cheese isn’t mandatory, but if you love an ice-cold filthy martini with a couple of blue cheese stuffed olives in it, you’ll totally understand my vision. Pair these with other Hanukkah favorites for a festive spread that's equal parts nostalgic and fun.

The latkes:Traditional latkes start with freshly grated potatoes, but frozen shredded hash browns are the secret shortcut here, cutting prep time without sacrificing crispy edges or fluffy centers. The key is squeezing out as much moisture as possible, then fluffing the shreds with a fork so they stay light instead of turning dense. Castelvetrano olives add a rich, buttery flavor, but Spanish queen or manzanilla olives work just as well. If you can find green olives already stuffed with pimento, go ahead and use them—you can skip the extra chopped pimentos altogether.

Make ahead & storage:The vermouth-blue cheese dipping sauce can be made up to 7 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator, making your day-of party prep that much easier. Leftover latkes can be refrigerated for up to 4 days; just reheat them in a 400° oven or air fryer until hot and crisp again for the best texture.

#6374. There’s an Actual Holiday for Eating Thanksgiving Leftovers Over the Kitchen Sink

A 1991 tuna salad snack started it all, and yes, there's a fan club.

It’s the morning after Thanksgiving. The good dishes are still drying, the fridge is a Tetris board of foil-wrapped leftovers and you’re standing over the kitchen sink eating cold stuffing with your bare hands. No plate, no judgment.

As it turns out, there’s an entire holiday dedicated to this very specific dining experience. It’s called Sinkie Day, and it’s been around since long before TikTok made girl dinner a thing.

For that, we have Norm Hankoff to thank. An advertising consultant from California, he had his lightbulb moment in 1991 “while wolfing down some tuna salad over his sink, using extra-strength potato chips as utensils,” according to a 1997 Associated Press report.

Convinced he couldn’t be the only one, Hankoff founded the International Association of People Who Dine Over the Kitchen Sink and declared the day after Thanksgiving Sinkie Day. By 1997, more than 1,000 people had joined, and each one received a membership certificate stamped with a double sink and the group’s motto: “Everybody does it. Sinkies proudly admit it.”

Naturally, there was a cookbook—or rather, a don’t-cook book. Published by a company cheekily called Digester’s Reader, The Official Sinkies Don’t Cook Book included such culinary masterpieces as “cakeless frosting” and “meat loaf in your fist.” Other recipes called for little more than a handful of mashed potatoes or a piece of chocolate cake dunked in a glass of milk.

Hankoff even set his sights on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. When Hillary Clinton was looking for a chef in 1994, he sent her a copy of his book and suggested the first family give sink-side snacking a try. No word on whether they took his advice, but the White House did send him a thank-you letter.

The beauty of Sinkie Day, which falls on Friday, Nov. 27, this year, is that it’s perhaps the only food holiday that actively encourages you to do less. A fridge full of Thanksgiving extras is all it takes, though a few upgrades never hurt:

Of course, a holiday devoted to leftovers is also a good excuse to brush up on food safety. As long as everything hit the fridge within two hours of cooking, you’ve got three to four days to work your way through it.

Are you a proud Sinkie? Let us know in the comments below!

#6373. We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

According to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

Moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He says that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

For gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

This is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

And if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

#6371. Sheet-Pan Thanksgiving Dinner

Whether you're hosting a small gathering this year or simply craving the comforting flavors of Thanksgiving any time of year, this sheet-pan dinner is the way to go. It’s a feast that’s as cozy as it is convenient, bringing together the classics with a few flavorful twists. The beauty of this meal lies in its simplicity—everything roasts together on a single pan, making cleanup a breeze.

The turkey:Using a bone-in split turkey breast helps ensure juicy, flavorful meat with rich, golden skin, slathered with butter and seasoned with poultry seasoning. This nod to tradition is enhanced with a touch of smoky paprika and garlic to amp up the flavors. For the stuffing, I went the classic route, using store-bought seasoned cubes for a bit of nostalgia, along with onions, celery, and soy sauce to boost the savory notes, and cranberries for a hint of sweetness. The stuffing offers the best of both worlds, with crispy edges and an irresistibly savory center soaked in turkey drippings.

The sweet potatoes:The sweet potatoes strike a perfect balance, spiced with warm and aromatic garam masala—a perfect pairing with the sweet yet earthy tuber. A splash of orange juice adds a tart-sweet touch, while pecans provide a satisfying crunch. If garam masala isn’t your thing, a dash of pumpkin pie spice works beautifully.

The green beans:The green beans, a nod to the iconic casserole, are streamlined for the sheet pan, tossed with mushrooms, Parmesan, and thyme-infused butter, and finished with crispy fried onions for that quintessential touch.

Make-ahead & storage:If the idea of making a whole Thanksgiving dinner on a sheet pan in one day feels daunting, here’s a tip—prep some components ahead of time. Most, if not all, of the ingredient chopping, grating, toasting, etc., can be done 2 to 3 days in advance. The stuffing can be made a day ahead; just be sure to cool it completely before refrigerating. Even the turkey can be buttered and seasoned the day before, leaving you with just the assembly and roasting on the day of.

#6370. Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 issue of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

#6368. This Restaurant Chain Was Just Named America’s Favorite

This beloved American fast-food chain is known for its ButterBurgers and frozen custard. Can you guess?

Pop the cheese curds, Wisconsin! Forbes just released its first-ever America’s Favorite Restaurants list, and the No. 1 spot didn’t go to Chick-fil-A, McDonald’s or any coastal cult favorite (lookin’ at you, In-N-Out). It went to Culver’s.

To build the ranking, Forbes partnered with data and insights company HundredX to poll more than 100,000 Americans about 100 restaurants, from sit-down chains and fast-food spots to coffee shops that serve food. The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

The Midwestern chain known for its ButterBurgers, frozen custard, crinkle-cut fries and breaded cheese curds scored extra well in taste and food quality. Honestly, anyone who’s ended a long day with a Concrete Mixer already knew that.

We’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

Culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the company is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

The biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. And if there’s not one nearby, these Culver’s copycats will do the trick.

#6366. Turkey in Mole Poblano

It may be called the great American bird, but turkey was first domesticated in Mexico, where, as James Beard once wrote, “it was to that country what beef is to the United States.” One of chef Rick Bayless’s favorite preparations is a celebratory dish from the Mexican state of Puebla: a slow braise of breast meat in a deep, dark mole that’s shot through with three kinds of dried chiles, studded with peanuts and pumpkin seeds, and enriched with chocolate and spices. The spicy, sweet, savory sauce can be sopped up with hot tortillas and rice, or even crusty bread.

#6365. This Clever Fork Trick Makes Slicing Cheese So Much Easier

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

As much as I love a big, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

One of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

Start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

This trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.

#6364. Maple Pumpkin Overnight Oats

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.)

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

#6363. Is It Rude to Bring Your Own Food to Thanksgiving?

Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

Thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

For the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host says dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

The short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:

I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a big breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

First, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a big deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

This is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really important to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

And I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really important for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

#6360. Giant Sheet-Pan Chocolate Almond Croissant

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.

This giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan. The bigger, the better, as they say, but we’re more into its shareable nature and simple-to-make design. Shatteringly crisp puff pastry (store-bought, of course) replaces hard-to-make croissant dough, with extra square footage for both this treat’s iconic croissant fillings: pain au chocolat and almond croissant. Win-win-win. Save this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant for special occasions or holiday mornings.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. On a lightly floured surface, roll out each sheet of puff pastry to a 12×10-inch rectangle. Place one on a parchment-lined 15x10x1-inch baking pan. Top the puff pastry with a second piece of parchment paper and a second 15x10x1-inch baking pan. This keeps the puff pastry from rising too much so it stays flat.

Bake the puff pastry for 15 minutes. Remove the top pan and parchment. Continue baking the puff pastry until it’s golden brown, five to seven minutes longer. Cool the puff pastry on a wire rack. Repeat the same process with the second slice of puff pastry.

Meanwhile, in a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, almond flour and confectioners’ sugar until they’re light and fluffy, two to three minutes. Add the egg and beat well until it’s incorporated.

Place one baked sheet of puff pastry on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Spread two-thirds of the almond filling over it.

Sprinkle the chocolate chips evenly all over. Carefully place the second sheet of baked puff pastry over top, and pipe or spread the remaining third of the almond filling on top.

Reduce the oven setting to 350°. Bake the croissant just until the filling is set, 18 to 20 minutes longer. Cool the croissant completely on a wire rack before serving.

Just as you’re ready to serve, dust the top with confectioners’ sugar and, if desired, drizzle it with warm hot fudge.

Store leftover giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant in an airtight container in the fridge. It can be kept for up to three days. Just know that it is best enjoyed the day of, as the frangipane will make the puff pastry soggy.

Yes, you can make certain aspects of a giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant ahead of time, but wait to assemble and bake it until you’re ready to serve. You can bake the puff pastry sheets one day ahead, let them cool to room temperature, wrap them tightly in storage wrap and store them at room temperature. Make the frangipane up to two days beforehand and keep it covered in the fridge.

Yes, you can make a gluten-free version of this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant. Simply replace the puff pastry with a gluten-free variety. DuFour, Sweet Loren’s and Schar make fantastic gluten-free puff pastry. All other ingredients are naturally gluten free (but do double-check the hot fudge, if you’re using it); just make sure they weren’t processed in a facility that handles wheat.

Serve your giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant with strong coffee or tea. Pair it with other brunch, like egg casseroles, plates of bacon and sausage and a fruit salad. I wouldn’t set out any other sweets—this croissant is plenty!

#6359. The Best Single-Serve Coffee Maker for All the Pod People Out There (2026)

Try as we might, there’s just no changing the hearts and minds of some people, even our dearest loved ones, by presenting them with inconvenient truths. I’m talking, of course, about people who prefer coffee from pods. But based on the popularity of coffee pod machines, it seems those of us who haven’t been assimilated into pod people are outnumbered. And, to be fair, even if the quality of their coffee is all over the place, we can’t deny their convenience. My goal here is to find single-serve coffee makers that can blend that convenience with coffee I actually want to drink.

In addition to plastic and aluminum pods, there’s a bevy of grounds-based coffee makers that specialize in one-cup-at-a-time brewing. So if you’re interested in the ease of pod machines, low-volume coffee brewing for one, or just can’t avoid K-cups, here are the machines that brewed the best.

Thanks to the revival of pour-over and French press coffee making and the proliferation of chic matte-finish electric kettles, there are plenty of ways to brew a single cup of coffee without a dedicated machine and, in general, they give you better results. We will also note that many fancier drip coffee makers (like our favorites from Fellow and Oxo) can now be programmed to brew just one cup of coffee at a time—and do so without the plastic waste of pods. If you want true versatility and have the counter space, we’d advise you to consider a machine that will let you brew for yourself or a crowd, if needed. But we understand the convenience factor of capsule machines, which is why, if you must pop a pod for your daily cup, we’ve made our recommendations below, plus suggested some non-pod options too.

Updated 11/25/26: Nespresso is phasing out it's old Vertuo Plus machines but never fear, the new Vertuo Up is an even better version of the original and it's our new top pick. And in other news, Keurig released its first completely K-Cup-free machine, and the new Alta platform is really quite good. That makes it the first Keurig machine we've ever recommended.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker

Size: 5” x 18" x 10.5”Water reservoir capacity: 47 oz.Colors: 4Coffee sizes: 1.3 oz., 2.7 oz., 5 oz., 8 oz., 12 oz., 18 oz.

What we love: Everything we loved about the original Nespresso Vertuo machine is present in the Vertuo Up. The centrifugal brewing method patented for Vertuo machines makes more balanced, better extracted coffee than most typical pod and capsule methods that just shower the grounds with water. And Nespresso continues to expand the world of capsules you can use, now featuring a number of single origin pods for those who prefer flavor profiles from different growing regions around the world, as well as flavored pods for folks whose regular Starbucks order is 13 words long.

And the Vertuo system also reads whatever capsule you insert and automatically brews at the proper volume, so it really does have one-button operation.

The rotating water tank is a nice touch because it allows the machine to fit in any configuration of kitchen and it's very easy to refill.

But the biggest upgrade is the addition of what Nespresso calls “Coffee Creation” mode, which is particularly good for iced coffee lovers. The extra button tells the machine to brew a more concentrated, smaller dose of coffee. That means it can melt the ice without diluting the flavor of the drink. It also lets you add a healthy pour of milk to hot coffee with the same results.

What we'd leave: Nespresso pods tend towards darker, roastier coffees. So if you have a thing for fruitier, more acidic coffee, you may be better off with either something that uses whole beans or Keurig's Alta.

Size: 10.84" W × 11.77" H × 19.0" DWater reservoir capacity: 72 ouncesColors: 3Coffee sizes: 1.5 oz. to 12 oz.

For a brand that’s name is pretty much synonymous with plastic pods, Keurig threw us for a loop in 2026 when it unveiled Alta, its first plastic pod-free system. Alta is still a single-serve machine and it still uses a capsule of sorts, swapping those little cups for AltaRounds, tablets of ground coffee held together by a compostable vegetable-based coating. Each AltaRound is printed with a QR code that tells the machine what drink styles it should offer up on the touchscreen display from said coffee, whether it is a smaller espresso tablet or a larger flavor coffee round.

What we love: In my experience, this is the first machine with any association to Keurig that I’ve actively enjoyed the coffee from and kept returning to. For contrast, the whole time I tested the Alta, I had my usual DeLonghi machine set up but a few feet away and for weeks I didn’t touch it because the coffee I really liked the coffee I got from the Alta. There were nuances between the different roasts, from light to medium to dark, and detectably different intensities in the espresso rounds. (Keurig’s announcement states that Peet’s coffee is already on board for future AltaRounds offerings and more partnerships are on the way.)

Customization, while usually limited to three dots indicating temperature and brew strength, was also effective, if a bit. When selecting a milk-based drink, the frother did an impressive job of adjusting to various temperatures and thicknesses, though I did find I usually had to scoop a good bit of any super airy cold foam or cappuccino foam from the pitcher with a spoon.

Navigating the menu was clear and easy. And once I got the hang of it, I found many aspects of the Alta, like the generous 72-ounce water tank and easy to empty drip and used coffee trays, or the simple swaps from hot to iced, to be seamless and a pleasure to use.

What we’d leave: First, it’s a large machine at 19 inches deep, occupying significant counter space, and while part of that has to do with the milk frothing apparatus, it’s also because the AltaRounds and separate K-cup slots are side-by-side, meaning if and when the brand just made the leap to an AltaRounds-only machine, it could probably be a good bit smaller. The automatic nature of the frother is handy, but pouring my own milk in a world of automatic dispensers on super-automatic espresso machines, left it up to me to set up the milk and do the pouring which may be more work than most Keurig converted coffee drinkers are used to. The generous water tank I called out above is slightly limiting in terms of where it allows you to set the machine up. It slides in or out from the side and if you don’t have space next to your Alta to do that, this could pose a problem. I also found the pours a bit splashy, and constantly had little droplets of coffee on the machine and on the counter nearby.

The touchscreen placement is a little wonky. It’s flat on top of the machine making it a little hard to read, and it’s actually housed in the lid for the AltaRounds slot, something that a new user (or houseguest) might not realize, as the K-cup slot is more readily discoverable with no screen and a lip for lifting it up. I fully put an AltaRound into the K-cup slot on the first go around before I more carefully read the instructions. This machine connects to WiFi, which is probably important for downloading new coffee brand specs as more AltaRounds become available, but my software updates were sometimes sticky and required unplugging the machine to unfreeze it.

Lastly, just to harp on the elephant plastic pod in the room, the Alta as it stands feels like a bridge machine to something better, but because of the sheer magnitude of the K-cup world Keurig has created, we’re stuck with a hybrid that feels part past and part future.

Size: 12.6"H x 4.5" W x 14" DWater reservoir capacity: 48 oz.Colors: Concrete, MidnightCoffee sizes: 4 oz., 6 oz., 8 oz., 10 oz., 12 oz.

What we love: If you’re looking for a streamlined, smart-looking machine to brew your K-cups, Chefman’s Caffeinator wraps its pod machine in a chic shell. There’s a snazzy drip tray that slides up and down for differently sized cups, and backlit touch buttons that disappear into the satin finish exterior (in Concrete or Midnight) when not selected. In addition to looking good, it also produced a pretty good cup of coffee, both from pods and grounds thanks to three simultaneous streams of water.

It offers a lot of customization possibilities, with three hot temperature options from “warm” to “piping hot” (the latter of which raised the temp about 20 degrees from default “hot”), plus a lower temp iced coffee mode, and three brew strengths in addition to multiple cup size selections. It's also compatible with both K-cups and ground coffee. All that gave me the ability to get my coffee a little closer to the way I want it, even if it comes from a plastic pod.

What we’d leave: Clearance for larger cups and tumblers is pretty low, unless you remove the drip tray entirely, which gives you 8.25" of height. But doing that leaves a ring and fixed “divot” about the width of a cupholder that some bigger travel mugs still may not fit into. I wish the water tank was a bit bigger, wasn’t rear-mounted, and had a sturdier lid, however it requires only a slight lift to remove it from the base so it’s easy to manage, even if you can’t see behind the machine. I would have also liked a place to store the K-cup/grounds adapter inserts when not using one or the other.

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker

Size: 15.71" H x 7.99" W x 11.47" DWater reservoir capacity: 58 oz.Color: Black Stainless (only one option)Coffee sizes: 8 oz., 10 oz., 12 oz., 16 oz., 20 oz., 24 oz.

What we love: Why settle for stale pods when you can have freshly ground coffee at the touch of a button? This single-serve machine from Cuisinart has a built-in stainless-steel conical burr grinder that grinds beans only when you’re ready for a cup of coffee. The bean hopper holds up to half a pound of coffee beans and has a gasket-sealed lid to keep them relatively fresh (a seemingly simple feature that my fancy grinder-equipped espresso machine lacks).

I was also impressed with the fineness of the sediment that was left in the bottom of my cup using the mesh filter. You should expect anything that uses only a mesh filter to leave at least a little bit of ground coffee sediment, but in this case it wasn’t unappealing during the last sips. If that is the sort of thing that bothers you, the basket is also paper filter compatible. Grinding and brewing are relatively quiet operations that probably won’t wake anyone up, and gentle beeps let you know your coffee is ready. Also, while you’ll need to find a carafe or container that fits under the machine, the fact that the Cuisinart can brew up to 24 oz. of hot coffee means you could, in a pinch, use this for a few guests over for brunch.

What we’d leave: Cleaning the filter after every use is a chore (and some people choose single-serve machines specifically to avoid that chore by using pods) That said, there are more gentle beeps to remind you the filter access door hasn’t been opened since the last brew, so at least you won’t forget. Clearance for cups, even with the drip tray completely removed, is still rather low for travel cups at just seven inches. Also, when brewing at the 24 oz. setting, the coffee was noticeably weaker than smaller cup sizes.

Size: 11.5" H x 7.5" W x 10.6" D (plus positionable water tank)Water reservoir capacity: 20-plus oz.Colors: Black, Linen (white)Coffee sizes: 5 oz.–20 oz.

What we love: Portland, Oregon–based Ratio takes its coffee maker design seriously, including its smallest entry, the Ratio Four, so named because it brews a maximum of four 5-oz. cups of coffee in a single batch. The machine couldn’t be simpler; it uses one button that brews however much water is in the reservoir and a filter basket with flat bottom paper filters. Turn it on, and the first of three lights illuminates to let you know it’s in Bloom mode, followed by Brew and Ready when your coffee is done. The Ratio heats brewing water to an average of 200º F and has a wide stainless-steel showerhead that evenly wets the coffee grounds, producing a full 20-oz. brew that was robust, strong, and exactly what I like to wake up to.

But we’re here to talk about single-serve coffee, and while using it for one cup is a little trickier (you’ll have to measure smaller quantities of water and coffee), the Four delivered the same bold, balanced brew in a 5-oz. cup, it did in a 20-oz. carafe. I found the recommended 9 grams of coffee lacking, but the instructions advise customizing the ratio a bit, and sure enough a few more grams in the filter did the trick. I found I got the tastiest results brewing two cups (10 oz.), as I think the longer siphoning and heating process with more water flowing through the system was key to a more satisfying extraction. Plus, I like a big cup of coffee.

The Ratio Four comes with a handblown 20-oz. glass carafe that also has a sealed lid and a silicone padded bottom. But what I appreciated is the ability to brew directly into any container; there is no hidden button or latch that the carafe needs to activate to brew or let water through. I could use a mug or travel tumbler if I wanted to. And, surprisingly, the same goes for the filter basket, with the Ratio website and instruction booklet explaining that they’d be just fine with you using it with a Kalita Wave or Origami pour-over dripper if you want. A long-press of the brew button also lets you choose between the default (4 oz. of water) bloom and a shorter (2 oz.) bloom, which is preferable if you are brewing a single cup.

All of the removable parts are hand-wash-only, but I never found them needing more than a rinse between uses. The instructions recommend occasional cleaning and descaling with an approved solution to keep the lines clean, though, which is important maintenance for any coffee maker.

It has an external, detached water tank that takes up more counter space than it would if it were flush with the machine, but that cuts both ways. I actually love that it’s connected via a sturdy yet flexible hose, allowing you to position it on either side of the machine in a variety of ways depending on your specific needs.

What we’d leave: Ratio is a brand known for machines with parts that feel very high quality, as senior editor Noah Kaufman has pointed out in his reviews of its other two machines. Some of the Ratio Four’s parts are definitely in line with that reputation, like the heavy braided hose between the brewer and water tank. But there are exterior parts of the brewer that do feel less substantial than you might expect for something that costs $279. I also found myself double-checking that the filter basket was installed correctly, because it doesn’t click or snap to signal it’s on right.

“Set it and forget it” coffee drinkers should take note that the water reservoir isn’t “smart,” meaning it will brew whatever water is inside, so a full reservoir with a coffee mug underneath will overflow. If that’s something you don’t want to think about, the Cuisinart Custom Grind and Brew might serve you better as it requires less frequent refills.

Size: 19" x 6" x 16"Water reservoir capacity: 80 oz.Colors: 2Coffee sizes: 2 oz., 10 oz.

What we love: We have an in-depth review of the Cumulus cold-brew machine for more details, but here’s the gist: You could, in some ways, consider this the Nespresso of cold coffee with its recyclable aluminum capsules that are filled an even more concentrated cold-brew concentrate. The machine does the job of chilling water via an onboard compressor, meaning you don’t need ice in your cup. For texture, the Cumulus offers three settings—still, nitro, and espresso—making it one of the best machines we’ve tried for cold coffee connoisseurs. (Oh, and it achieves that “nitro” coffee without any gas canisters by using ambient air.) It vacuums out the capsules, leaving them empty and ready to recycle after you’re done brewing. And at just 6", wide it’s got a relatively small footprint and front-loading water reservoir, making it easy to use and keep on the countertop.

What we’d leave: At its current nearly $700 price tag, this is a luxury item—though, if you’re dropping $5 on cold brew every day, maybe it isn’t?

With so many brands and varieties of pods out there, I did my best to compare apples to apples by using Starbucks pods and beans of the same roast for every machine (Bruvi being the only exception that doesn’t sell Starbucks pods). That’s not because the global corporate coffee giant is my favorite coffee roaster, but because it is the most cross-pollinated among all types of machines and formats. For Keurig machines, I also tested using K-cups from Illy coffee, which I’ve found produce stronger coffee (an attribute testers often flag as missing from Keurigs). I used fresh grounds for any machines that offered a refillable pod and whole beans of the same roast were used on machines with grinding capabilities. I also tested the different brew size, strength, and style options on any machine with multiple settings.

There are plenty of subpar single-cup coffee makers out there, and life is short, so we don’t think bad coffee needs to be a part of it. We looked for coffee pod machines that delivered balanced flavor and a smooth finish with consistency.

Are the pods simple to load and is the interface (buttons or screens) intuitive and simple? Does the water reservoir require constant refill oversight, and is it easy to access? Does the machine require regular cleaning or maintenance to keep working? The ease of use should extend to pod collection and disposal as well. Some machines require emptying the coffee pod chamber after each use. Others collect them for occasional disposal or recycling.

Pod coffee makers don’t need to take up too much space, but they can also be too small, relying on heating and brewing elements that sacrifice on quality. And because most regular coffee drinkers won’t be putting their machine away every day, it should look good on your countertop too.

Pods are a problem. There’s no way around it. No coffee brewing option will be as ecologically sound as simply pouring water over grounds (and then composting those grounds if you can). Yes, technically you can tear apart Keurig pods, empty their spent coffee into your compost bin and the filter into the trash, and then recycle the plastic cup portion. But overall, we can’t get behind any machine that requires plastic pods that aren’t easily recyclable. Machines that operate using a reusable pod were also given some bonus points.

You’d be hard-pressed to find a better looking coffee machine than the Terra Kaffe Demi. It’s stylish, it comes in four colors, and it’s relatively small for something with a built-in grinder at just over 7" wide—however, it’s nearly 16" deep, and you’ll need access to both sides of the machine, plus the reservoir housed on the back. (If you opt for the milk-frothing TK-02 option, it’ll be wider and deeper still.) Aside from brewing great espresso and pretty great coffee, the most impressive aspect of the Terra Kaffe is how quiet it is. Compared to the cacophony my similarly priced grind-and-brew automatic espresso machine makes, the Demi barely produced a sound.

Generally, I liked the espresso results I got from the Terra Kaffee more than I liked the drip coffee. Once I dialed in my preferred drip settings—which you can adjust for any of the machine’s four drink presets after navigating a maze of menus and submenus—I was impressed with the rich flavor and texture of the coffee with no hint of sediment at the bottom of the cup. For what’s essentially a super-automatic espresso machine with no milk frothing, it’s expensive (commitment-phobes can rent it for $40 a month), so it wouldn’t be my first choice to simply fill a mug in the morning. But if you toggle back and forth between coffee and espresso, it’s comparably priced with other super automatic machines, and it offers a sleek and almost silent option.

This touchscreen pod machine is everything we wish most K-cup machines could be. It offers rich, balanced, and nuanced coffee, plus eight brewing sizes, one-touch presets for low-acid, americano, iced coffee (which brews hot over ice), and cold brew (which uses cooler water), as well as simple customizations to any of these like temperature control and brew strength. And it does all this using its own proprietary pods made with specially treated polypropylene, which will (mostly) break down in a landfill. So other than you need to use its proprietary coffee pods, Bruvi offers all of the convenience of capsules and the fancy-pants settings of high-end coffee makers and good coffee with little downside.

An espresso machine but make it Nespresso. That’s the idea behind the Creatista series from Nespresso, which adds the automatic milk steaming perfected by Breville, bootstraps it on to a Nespresso Vertuo machine, and wraps the whole thing in handsome stainless steel. It’s great for someone looking for a cappuccino hack. Ultimately we picked the Keurig Alta over the Creatista for this genre of machine because it’s a little less expensive and offers a little more versatility in the form of cold foam options.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville

The Vertuo Plus does everything the Vertuo Up does sans the iced coffee and full carafe brewing features. The big knock on it is that it's being phased out to make way for several other Vertuo machines. But it's still available from third party retailers like Williams Sonoma and Amazon right, often for pretty affordable prices.

The Essenza Mini comes from Nespresso’s Original line, which uses smaller capsules and only brews 1.35-oz. espresso shots or 3.7-oz. Lungo cups of coffee. And it does so using 19 bars of pressure for extraction, as opposed to the VertuoLine’s centrifugal extraction method. It doesn’t make plain old cups of coffee, however, but we’ve included it here as a good option for pod coffee drinkers who prefer espresso drinks and want a simple way to make beverages like cappuccinos and macchiatos.

Like its larger Moccamaster brethren, Cup-One has a timeless, old-school design and a single, tactile glowing “on” switch would make it look at home in a truck stop diner or a trendy modern apartment. And speaking of diners, the coffee, even in a 10-oz. default brew, was diner quality (I mean that affectionately), with robust flavor and texture—though that may have had something to do with the fact that I used the recommended four tablespoons of grounds, twice what other machines suggest for eight oz. Considering its higher price tag, it appears to be pretty low-tech. Okay, okay, it’s just an automatic pour-over machine. But it brewed one of the best single cups from grounds I’ve had from any drip machine. And it’s quiet with no bubbling or burping. What can I say? The small footprint and retro vibes also won me over. It’s a small luxury. It’s a vibe. As the kids say, it’s aesthetic.

Now for the minuses: Yes, you could get a (really nice) gooseneck kettle and pour-over system for, like, half the cost. Give and take. Low clearance under the drip spout means you’re stuck with brewing into mugs and low-profile tumblers. The included measuring scoop and a needle-like poking tool for clearing the filter holder have no home onboard the machine, adding to your “things we need to keep but don’t know where else to put” drawer.

Of all the podless machines, this one is the most podlike in its convenience while producing pod-beating coffee. The eponymous Scoop is a small mesh filter that doubles as a measuring spoon. Just scoop up (or in) your grounds to the maximum fill line, and you’re good to go. The Scoop sits in a second “grounds catching” mesh filter which, in my tests, reduced silt in my cup compared to similar single-filter systems, but didn’t eliminate it. Using the two size settings, you can brew either 8 oz. or 14 oz. per cup. The coffee it produced on normal brew mode was fine, but tapping the BOLD setting did actually produce much more robust results. However, each cup I made was on the oily side.

A flip-down drip tray holds standard mugs, while the lower drip tray has a clearance of 7", so lots of travel tumblers stand a chance. The 40-oz. water reservoir is on the small side, but is easy to access and lift off from either side with a molded-in handle.

When you’re done, simple empty and rinse The Scoop (filter) and, if necessary, the secondary filter, and you can brew another cup right away. That’s as long as your Scoop filter is dry, anyway. If it’s still damp from the last cup, you’re going to need to scoop into The Scoop, which basically just makes this like any other small filter machine.

4-in-1 Single-Serve Latte, Iced, and Hot Coffee Maker

When you think of Mr. Coffee, you probably think of a basic, no-frills drip machine sitting on your grandparents’ countertop. And, for the most part, this multifunction machine is still just a small, simple rain-shower-style drip coffee maker designed for one-cup-at-a-time brewing. The reservoir and reusable mesh filter sit under the lid and feature graduated measurements for water levels from 4 oz. up to 16 oz. You can fill the removable filter with grounds using a double-ended measuring scoop that nests on the side of the machine and has guidelines for different sizes and styles of coffee, whether you’re brewing a “shot” for milk-based drinks or a tumbler full of iced coffee. The bonus of this machine is that, while still retaining a small footprint, it also includes a decent self-contained, stainless-steel milk frother cup with presets for hot milk and cold foam that can be used completely independently from the coffee-making portion.

As for taste and texture, everything was like middle-of-the-road drip coffee. However, I found that following the instructions for the weakest iced coffee (one large scoop) actually gave me decent results that weren’t as watered down as other machines on this list. It also comes with a 22-oz. plastic tumbler just for iced coffee—and enough brewing clearance to fit such a large cup—so if you’re someone who flip-flops between iced and hot coffee and aren’t too finicky about dialing in precise strength, it’s a practical option.

If, for whatever reason, you want to brew Nespresso pods but don’t want to actually get a Nespresso machine, the L’or is your choice. It brews Original Nespresso pods along with its own proprietary pods (which are cross-compatible with classic Nespresso machines). L’or’s brewer offers three brewing sizes and extracts coffee from the pod at 19 bars of pressure through two spouts, similar to the way coffee comes out of a semiautomatic espresso machine. This produces a delicious layer of crema that’s as good as Nespresso’s. It was only in a head-to-head matchup that we slightly preferred Nespresso.

If you like the idea of Nespresso but not the idea of being stuck with one-cup-at-at-time brewing, the Vertuo Next has brew sizes ranging from a single shot of espresso up to 18 oz. of coffee with the proper pods (an optional carafe is available for the biggest brews). This smart machine also has Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, so you can track your favorite pods and get firmware updates. However, the Next is a smaller machine than the Vertuo Plus, and with that comes a smaller water tank. And like the Vertuo Pop+ below, the closing and locking mechanism is a bit clunkier than we’d like. But for all out versatility, it’s probably your best Nespresso brewing option.

If you’re looking for a K-cup-compatible coffee machine that can do a little more, this is a good option. It comes with a reusable filter capsule that, while a little finicky getting it to work properly, does, indeed, work. It also has a 72-oz. water tank for less-frequent refills, as well as settings for five cup sizes and two brewing temperatures. The biggest boost we’ll give this machine is that it produced superior tasting coffee using K-cups than any Keurig machine we’ve tried.

We like almost all Nespresso machines, but we think the three recommended above are better than the Vertuo Pop+ for a few reasons. On the Pop+, the actual snapping down of the lid to puncture the pod inside was the clunkiest of the bunch and a lot of effort in a pre-coffee morning fog. And this low-profile machine was so low to the counter, we couldn’t fit a pint glass or similarly sized tumbler underneath, which was a problem considering that Nespresso offers Iced Leggero pods that brew 7.7 oz., overflowing our smaller ice-filled cups. Lastly, the water reservoir on the standard version of this machine (which comes in at 25.4 oz. or 32 oz. on the Deluxe model) is pretty small compared to the Vertuo Plus, and it’s set in a fixed side-mounted position, so you’re stuck with the orientation as is. In other words, it’s still a solid Nespresso coffee brewer but less versatile than what you get for a few dollars more.

You might consider this machine Lavazza’s attempt to answer the classic Nespresso; its plastic coffee pods and presets brew in espresso or lungo sizes. It beats the Keurig and K-cup machines when it comes to robust and flavorful coffee, but it didn’t live up to the high bar set by Nespresso. The Ristretto capsules we tried were a bit bitter and the texture was thin, though we actually liked the medium-roast decaf capsules enough as after dinner/dessert coffee. Considering Lavazza makes capsules for both Nespresso classic machines and K-cup machines, along with other espresso products, we just don’t think it’s necessary to buy into the Lavazza tech—as sleek and compact as it is—to enjoy its coffee.

The dual on this machine refers to both drip coffee and coffee pods. It offers multiple brew sizes and strengths, and, being a drip machine first, comes with a glass carafe. It accepts pods with an adapter that fits into the filter basket. Some of its handier features are an adjustable 60-oz. water reservoir, dedicated hot water dispenser, fold-away milk frother, and an adjustable drip tray that allows you to brew directly into a cup or tumbler. But we don’t think it’s the best drip coffee maker out there, and it’s too big and complex for just making capsule coffee.

There’s a lot to like about the exterior design of this slimmed down version a Ninja single-serve system, from its pleasing colorways like stone, sage green, and glacier blue (in addition to black), its handy fold-away frothing wand that easily whipped some pre-warmed milk into a mug full of foam, or its storage nooks for the pod/grounds adapters and measuring spoon. The generous water tank, while rear-mounted, has a pressure fit lid that actually stays put between the faucet and counter. And all of its detachable parts and pieces are dishwasher-safe. But whether you’ll crave the actual coffee from this machine is another story. Pods tasted weak, even at the lower 6-oz. brewing size, and grounds were better but not by very much. The Specialty Brew setting, which brews a 4-oz. shot of coffee for use with the frother, isn’t quite an espresso experience, either. And while you can choose multiple cup sizes, you can’t select anything but the preset temperature.

Despite its 4.4 stars from over 100,000 ratings on Amazon, we can’t imagine using this machine for coffee every day. Our experience with Keurig coffee pods, regardless of the brand of coffee we tried, was watery or bitter coffee (or, at worst, somehow both). That, plus the fact that this machine’s reservoir is only large enough for one cup at a time makes this one tedious for regular use.

Unfortunately, the “smart” features of this machine add more frustration than anything. The machine is supposed to recognize which K-cup you put inside and adjust its brew settings accordingly. It also allows you to select and save brew sizes and temperatures as presets. But in our tests, the machine frequently froze and had to be unplugged to get it going again. Being “smart,” this machine also offers app-enabled remote brewing, something we can’t imagine using since you have to put K-cups in (and take used cups out) one at a time. One plus was the generous 66-oz. water reservoir with a convenient pitcher handle. But in the end, this fancy Keurig didn’t improve our pod coffee experience whatsoever.

As iced coffee rivals hot coffee consumption these days, it’s no wonder Keurig would offer a machine that specializes in cold drinks. One aspect of this machine that’s well thought-out is its dispensing spout, which is high enough off the counter to accommodate a pint glass or tumbler. We found the iced coffee setting only reduced the brew temperature by less than 10°, so our ice still had to do most of the work while also watering the coffee down, which was already diluted with 12 oz. of water during brewing. Even on the smallest of three preprogramed hot coffee brew sizes, it mirrored our other Keurig experiences with weak or just not tasty coffee output.

Oxo 8-cup Coffee Maker with Podless Single Serve Function

Even though this is an 8-cup coffee maker, I tested this machine because it proudly advertises on the box that it’s also a single-serve machine. Let me get one thing out of the way immediately: This is a great little drip coffee maker if you’re brewing by the carafe. It has the option to brew full and half carafes, and a heated warming plate that keeps the coffee pleasantly hot for hours. But it fell short on a few functional aspects, as well as that single-serve option. First, the water tank is not “smart”—as in, it uses all the water you put in it every time. So if you want a full carafe, you fill it all the way up with water, and if you want a single cup, you put in just enough for… two cups. No, it doesn’t actually brew a single serving of coffee. For a $200-plus machine purporting to do single-serve brewing that can go toe-to-toe with Keurig, that’s a little disappointing.

Additional testing and reporting by Emily Farris

#6358. I Tried Ina Garten’s Ranch Dressing, and It Changed My Mind About Ranch

I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing. Then I made Ina's version.

I have a confession to make. I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing. I realize this puts me at odds with a substantial portion of the American population, but I’ve always preferred a good balsamic vinaigrette or a creamy Caesar. And despite making countless salad dressings over the years, I’ve never once felt compelled to make ranch.

I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch. I found the whole business unappealing, an opinion that has apparently skipped a generation seeing as both of my children now do exactly the same thing. There’s always a bottle of ranch in our refrigerator that was purchased specifically for pizza night, and it has absolutely nothing to do with me.

Then I came across an Instagram reel of Ina Garten making her buttermilk ranch dressing for a wedge salad. I’ve trusted Ina with everything from roast chicken to panna cotta, and if anyone could persuade me to reconsider my longstanding position on ranch, I figured it would be her. So, after decades of avoiding it, I finally made a batch of ranch dressing.

Ina’s recipe makes about 3 cups of dressing, which initially struck me as an ambitious quantity for someone with my history of distatte. Fortunately, it comes together in just a few minutes, and the ingredients are far more fresh and interesting than anything I’d previously associated with ranch.

Combine the scallions, basil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, olive oil, garlic, salt and pepper in a food processor fitted with a steel blade. Puree them for 15 to 20 seconds, until the mixture is smooth.

Add the mayonnaise, Greek yogurt and buttermilk, then blend the dressing again until everything is thoroughly combined. Transfer the dressing to a covered container and refrigerate it for an hour to let the flavors develop.

That’s really all there is to it. No complicated technique or careful emulsifying, and very little cleanup. The hour in the refrigerator is important, though, since it gives the garlic, herbs and other seasonings time to mingle with the creamy ingredients.

Of course, I expected Ina’s ranch to be better than the bottled varieties I’ve tried. What I didn’t expect was for it to taste like an entirely different dressing.

The first thing that struck me was how fresh it was. The basil and scallions give it a wonderful, almost garden-like quality, while the garlic and Dijon add savory sharpness that keeps all that creaminess interesting. There’s plenty of richness from the mayonnaise, but the buttermilk, Greek yogurt and lemon juice provide enough acidity to balance it. It’s tangy, herbaceous and wonderfully flavorful—without the heavy, slightly cloying quality I’ve always associated with ranch.

And the basil! It’s not an herb I would have thought to put in ranch dressing, but it works beautifully. Its flavor comes through clearly without overwhelming the other ingredients, giving the dressing a character all its own.

In her video, Ina serves the dressing over a wedge salad topped with tomatoes and onion. Having already entrusted her with the dressing, I figured I might as well follow her lead with the salad, too. I made my own wedge with Flavor Bombs tomatoes (my favorites), pepitas and crispy pieces of bacon, then spooned a generous amount of ranch over the whole thing. The cold, crunchy lettuce was the perfect backdrop for the dressing, while the sweet tomatoes, salty bacon and nutty pepitas made the whole thing particularly satisfying. I’ve always loved a good wedge salad, but this was easily one of the best I’ve had.

By the time I’d finished testing and photographing the recipe, nearly half the dressing was gone, and I was already making plans for the rest. I have to admit, I’m even curious to see how it tastes with pizza, which is not something I ever expected to say about ranch dressing.

#6357. Cottage Cheese Meatballs

Recipe by Lauren Habermehl, Pewaukee, Wisconsin

No ricotta? Reach for a scoop of protein-rich cottage cheese. It's the secret to these tender, moist and protein-rich meatballs.

My kids have never been huge meat eaters. In fact, my son is more likely to polish off a giant bowl of cherry tomatoes than he is to dig into a burger. Meatballs, though, have always been the exception—and these cottage cheese meatballs have been a long-time favorite. My kids love how tender and juicy they are, and I love that they sneak a little extra protein into their diet.

Many traditional meatball recipes already include ricotta cheese, which binds and adds moisture to the meat mixture. Cottage cheese is a natural swap, adding fat that keeps the meatballs irresistibly moist and tender. Once these protein-packed meatballs are simmered in your favorite jarred pasta sauce and served over pasta, people will never guess that cottage cheese is the secret ingredient.

Editor’s Tip: For the softest, most tender meatballs, handle them gently as you shape them. Avoid overhandling or compacting the meat too much (one of Grandma’s best meatball tips), as it can make the meatballs tough and dense.

#6355. Homemade Turkey Stock

Turkey stock is a must-make if you had turkey as your Thanksgiving centerpiece. You don't want to let those scraps go to waste, do you? Throw in some of those wilting herbs and whatever carrots and celery you have on hand to make a great pantry staple. It takes almost zero effort and leaves you with a flavorful stock that you can store in the freezer until you're ready to put it to use.

You can make basically anything you'd make with chicken stock (which is a lot!) with this stock. One of the best uses of turkey stock is turkey gravy and that can be used to top something like poutine or stuffing. Or you can make a time-tested classic Turkey Tetrazzini. Whatever you do, don't let this stock go to waste.

Add all of the ingredients to a large stockpot. Cover turkey completely with water, about 10 to 12 cups.

Over medium heat, bring the stockpot to a boil, then reduce heat and let it simmer for 3 hours. Spoon fat off the top as it rises.

Strain stock through a fine mesh strainer. Let the stock cool to room temperature.

Store in refrigerator until ready to use for up to 2 weeks or in the freezer for 3 months.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Stock is the perfect thing to store in your freezer! After letting your stock cool to room temp you can store in the refrigerator for 2 weeks or in the freezer for up to 3 months. Set it out in the fridge the night before you plan to use to defrost or place it in a pan of barely simmering water to thaw out quickly!

#6354. Jif’s Surprising New Product at Costco Has Nothing to Do with Sandwiches

Hold the jelly! The iconic peanut butter brand is taking a surprisingly savory direction with its latest product.

Who says peanut butter doesn’t deserve a spot in your dinner rotation?

Jif, the beloved peanut butter brand that’s been a staple in American pantries for decades, has ventured into some unexpected territory. If you’re a frequent Costco shopper, you might want to take a closer look the next time you’re browsing the instant noodles.

Some locations of the warehouse retailer are now carrying a six-pack of Jif stir-fry-style instant ramen noodles, giving shoppers an entirely different way to enjoy the taste of peanut butter.

But so far, the reviews among shoppers are mixed.

“Anyone who thinks this sounds gross has never had Thai food and it shows. Peanut butter noodles are kinda awesome,” one fan wrote in a video making the rounds on Instagram.

“Prolly fire w some chili oil,” another claimed.

“I had this last month. Pretty good for instant noodles,” another said.

A fourth wrote, “As a peanut butter [connoisseur] I don’t approve this.”

“Diabolical waste of resources,” a fifth claimed.

Peanuts have long been incorporated into savory noodle dishes, particularly in Asian-inspired cooking. Still, seeing the recognizable Jif logo on a package of instant noodles might have you raising your eyebrows. Rather than replicating the sweet, creamy taste of a spoonful of peanut butter, the noodles take a more savory approach. The seasoning contains peanut flour alongside ingredients like soy sauce, garlic and artificial beef flavor.

Jif has another product worth keeping an eye out for at Costco. The brand’s peanut butter and chocolate pretzel Snappers hit shelves in October and offer a sweet-and-salty alternative for those who aren’t quite sold on the noodles.

As always, product availability can vary by warehouse, so it’s worth checking your warehouse’s stock online before making a special trip. You can also buy the Jif instant ramen at Walmart or Amazon.

But the real question is, would you give peanut butter ramen a try, or is this one food crossover you’ll happily sit out?
