#6307. Security Footage Catches Two Zoo Gorillas Forming a “Living Ladder” To Outsmart an Electric Fence

Two zoo gorillas repeatedly teamed up for food despite rarely spending time together, showing that a shared effort does not always end with a shared meal.

A leafy branch was out of reach for two gorillas at the Ramat Gan Safari, and an electric barrier around the trunk blocked a direct climb. The female western lowland gorillas, half-sisters Amelia and Lisha, formed a “living ladder,” with Lisha providing a steady back for Amelia to stand on.

The most extensively documented event came to light in September 2024, when keepers noticed the pair peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach. Staff reviewed security camera footage to find out how they had obtained it.

The recording showed Amelia walking over and climbing onto a rock beneath a Peltophorum dubium tree. Lisha joined her and stood firmly on all fours on the rock. Amelia then climbed onto Lisha’s back, stood upright, and reached up to grasp and break off a branch approximately 4.5 meters, or 15 feet, above the ground. The rock, Lisha’s stable posture, and Amelia’s reach together made the branch accessible.

Researchers documented three events involving the same pair in 2021, 2024, and 2025, with each gorilla performing the same role every time. Neither had been trained to perform the maneuver. The team describes their behavior as a rare example of spontaneous cooperation between adult gorillas, with a clear division of roles.

Published in Primates, the study was led by Michael Levitzky and Prof. Israel Hershkovitz of the Department of Anatomy and Anthropology at the Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences and the Dan David Center for Human Evolution and Biohistory Research at Tel Aviv University.

Yehonatan Samocha, Head of the Primate Section at the Ramat Gan Safari (Zoological Center Tel Aviv-Ramat Gan), said, “At the Ramat Gan Safari we have observed and studied animal behaviors for years, closely following their relationships, social bonds, and fascinating capabilities. Particularly among great apes, including gorillas, we repeatedly encounter behaviors that demonstrate high intelligence, learning ability, problem-solving, complex communication, and cooperation.

“This is why we are so thrilled, though not necessarily surprised, by the cooperation between Amelia and Lisha. We are familiar with their abilities and understand how intelligent and curious they are, and how capable they are of learning from one another and working together. Sometimes, our surprise tells us more about our expectations of animals than their actual abilities. The study’s great importance lies in providing scientific documentation and analysis for observations and behaviors we encounter in our daily work, allowing us to enhance our knowledge of gorillas, their social world, and their cognitive abilities.”

In the June 2025 footage, Lisha positioned herself with her back toward Amelia, who was not observed using force. Levitzky, who initiated and led the study, explained how the recording helped the researchers interpret Lisha’s participation.

“When I first watched the footage, it was clear to me that this was something extraordinary. What I find fascinating is that Leisha did more than simply serve as a ‘step’ for Amelia. She appeared to participate actively and willingly in solving the problem, approaching on her own initiative and positioning herself in exactly the right place, without Amelia physically guiding her. This is the difference between using another individual as a tool and true cooperation, in which both individuals work together toward the same goal.

“For years, gorillas were considered less cognitively sophisticated than other great apes. As more observations like these accumulate, we will be able to deepen and refine our understanding of their social and cognitive abilities. Future studies involving systematic documentation and audio recordings could help us decipher how they coordinate with one another, and perhaps also teach us something about the roots of cooperation in our own species.”

The sisters generally spend little time together, sleep in separate night quarters, and rarely groom one another. Their teamwork also had different outcomes at feeding time. Although keepers reported peaceful sharing after the 2024 event, Amelia alone ate the vegetation in the observed 2025 sequence, showing that cooperating to obtain food did not necessarily lead to sharing it.

Hershkovitz said, “Our observations reveal how two gorillas can join forces and assume complementary roles to solve a problem that neither can solve on her own. It is particularly intriguing that this cooperation recurs even though the two do not usually display much closeness, and even when the food is not shared between them afterward. These observations are important for understanding human evolution because they offer an explanation, albeit a partial one, for how we survived on the savanna – through social support and a high level of cooperation that can occur even without language or preplanning. Although the number of observations is small, they offer a window into gorillas’ ability to learn from experience, coordinate their actions, and draw on one another and their surroundings to achieve a shared goal.”

The study involved only two gorillas and three documented events. The available footage could not establish whether they communicated through vocalizations or subtle gestures, or whether they planned their actions in advance.

Reference: “Cooperation in adult female western lowland gorillas: complex problem-solving through learned spatial affordances and mutual agency” by Michael Levitzky, and Israel Hershkovitz, 24 October 2026, Primates. DOI: 10.1007/s10329-026-01297-6

#6306. Seabirds named George and Geraldine returned for their 10th anniversary as a couple

Short-tailed albatrosses George and Geraldine returned to Midway Atoll for their 10th year together, offering hope for this endangered species.

Two short-tailed albatrosses known as George and Geraldine are back on Sand Island at Midway Atoll, which lies in the North Pacific.

Their arrival was confirmed in late October 2026, marking the 10th straight year the two have returned as a pair, according to the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP).

ACAP describes them as the only short-tailed albatrosses breeding in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Together they have raised and fledged at least five chicks.

Both birds were banded as chicks on Japan’s Torishima island. George hatched there in 2003 and has visited Midway since November 2006, when he was known as “Lonesome George.”

Geraldine is thought to be a bird banded on Torishima in April 2008. She was first seen on Midway in early 2012, ACAP reported in 2024.

The two were first seen together in late 2016 and first shared a nest the following season.

That 2017/18 season, they incubated an egg laid by a black-footed albatross, and the chick fledged. Black-footed and Laysan albatrosses also nest on Sand Island.

Geraldine’s sex was still listed as unconfirmed in 2018. She settled the question by laying the egg the two incubated in October 2023.

Before them, another short-tailed pair raised chicks on Midway’s Eastern Island, most recently in 2013/14. Its male was found dead there in November 2014.

George and Geraldine’s own first chick hatched on Jan. 3, 2019, and biologists banded it that May. It left its nest site earlier than expected, in late May, and became the first chick known to fledge from Sand Island.

Short-tailed albatross chicks hatch from late December through January, and each breeding cycle lasts about eight months.

Their next chick left in 2020. It walked across Sand Island before taking off over the water, likely to spend five or more years at sea.

“Nature has a way of reminding us that species and populations often have a remarkable capacity for resilience and fuel our hopes for recovering natural systems,” said Jonathan Plissner, then an island restoration specialist at Island Conservation, in 2020.

Not every season has worked. The 2021/22 egg did not hatch.

A chick that fledged in 2022/23 returned in April 2024 and displayed with one hatched in 2019/20. That November, two of their earlier chicks were photographed within a few feet of Geraldine as she incubated.

In late 2024, a fifth short-tailed albatross was also on Sand Island. The sub-adult, nicknamed Forest Bird, came from the same Torishima cohort as Geraldine and lived alone about a mile (1.6 kilometers) from the others.

George and Geraldine had no success in 2024/25. They bred again in 2025/26, when eight different short-tailed albatrosses were recorded on the atoll, three of them their offspring.

Those returning young birds may eventually start breeding on Midway themselves.

In Hawaiian, the short-tailed albatross is called makalena. Around the turn of the 20th century, feather hunters killed millions of them, nearly wiping out the species, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS).

The agency listed the species as endangered throughout its range in 2000. A 2020 review estimated the population at 7,365 birds, growing about 8.9 percent a year.

It is the largest albatross in the North Pacific, with wings spanning about 7 to 7.5 feet (213 to 229 centimeters).

Short-tailed albatrosses begin breeding at five or six years old. Parents take turns on the egg and alternate foraging trips that can last two to three weeks.

Torishima, the main colony, is an active volcano. In 2010, a landslide there buried up to ten chicks.

Between 2008 and 2012, chicks moved from Torishima to Mukojima started a third colony.

These albatrosses spend most of their lives at sea, ranging from China and Japan to Russia, Alaska and Canada. The highest concentrations occur around the Aleutian Islands and in the Bering Sea.

Birds that follow fishing boats can be hooked or tangled in longline gear and drown. Albatross chicks can also choke and die after eating plastic.

On land, Midway brings its own threat. Mice were first seen attacking albatrosses on the atoll in December 2015.

The Midway Seabird Protection Project spread bait across Sand Island by helicopter on July 20 and 21, 2023. Crews also scattered bait by hand in sensitive areas and used bait boxes around buildings.

By Aug. 15, mice were still being found, and eradication efforts were stopped.

The project then moved into what the USFWS calls a “Mitigation and Learning Phase.” A similar attempt on Gough Island also failed to remove mice that attack albatrosses and other seabirds.

The information was obtained from the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels.

#6305. America’s Data Centers Have a Hidden Death Toll, MIT Researchers Warn

An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.

As artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension. The electricity needed to keep these facilities running around the clock can increase air pollution in communities far from where the data centers themselves are built, potentially putting the health of people who live nowhere near them at risk.

Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone. Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas had the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita, even though much of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Rates in Virginia and Texas were only about half those in most Midwestern states.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, senior author of the study, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), and director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers’ electricity needs accounted for about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and approximately 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. Those proportions have likely grown as more facilities have been built.

Determining who bears the health consequences of that growing demand is complicated by the interconnected nature of the nation’s power grid. A data center in Virginia, for example, may increase electricity production at power plants in the Ohio Valley, where a greater proportion of older coal and natural gas plants produce higher levels of emissions.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

The pollution can then travel into neighboring states, where local atmospheric conditions can make matters worse. In agricultural regions such as Iowa and Nebraska, ammonia released from fertilizer promotes the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), microscopic airborne particles that can cause heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

The estimated health consequences also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas. Overall, the researchers found that rural populations face a significantly higher estimated mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations.

To understand how these risks are distributed, the team developed a model that tracks electricity production and transmission between regions on an hourly basis. While many previous studies relied on average power grid emissions, the researchers assumed that data centers operated around the clock and identified which individual generators would respond to their additional electricity needs.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” says Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student and co-author of the study.

“It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”

The researchers calculated emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide from individual generators. Both pollutants contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter, while nitrogen oxides also help produce ground-level ozone, commonly associated with smog.

Using a separate atmospheric model, the team simulated how these pollutants formed and traveled across regions. They then drew on epidemiological research linking air pollution to premature death to estimate the resulting health impacts.

Of the approximately 650 premature deaths estimated for 2023, 513 were attributed to fine particulate matter and 137 to smog. Together, they represented about 5.3 percent of all estimated electricity-related premature deaths nationwide.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin says.

As companies continue to expand their computing infrastructure, the findings suggest that decisions about where to build data centers and how to power them need to account for public health well beyond the immediate surroundings.

“When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” Chen says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”

The researchers hope to investigate the air quality consequences of a growing industry trend in which data centers incorporate their own on-site power plants. They could also examine whether adjusting when these facilities consume electricity could reduce their impact on air quality.

Reference: “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States” by Yuang Chen, Shen Wang, Juan Ramon L Senga, Andrew Scott White, Anthony YH Wong, Lyssa M Freese, Michelle L Bell and Noelle E Selin, 19 November 2026, Environmental Research Letters. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aebbd4

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

#6304. The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea. However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI.

First, letâs dig into what the back-of-the-envelope calculations say. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests that U.S.-based data centers could consume 580 terawatt-hours of electricity over a five-year window, an increase of around 17-46 gigawatts compared to modern levels. But land-based data centers are running into plenty of bottlenecks, from newly elected hostile politicians to hard caps on the electrical gridâs ability to supply all that additional power.

So the solution seems obvious - launch the data centers into orbit, where they will be beyond any individual NIMBY protesters, have access to essentially unlimited free solar power, and not have to deal with water cooling systems. Sounds pretty good. Until the actual physics of what that means comes into play.

Fraser addresses the idea of data centers in space.

There are three main physics hurdles that all culminate into a giant economic one facing data centers, and it all comes down to scale. Size and weight are the first major obstacle. Dr. Turyshev uses a baseline 1-megawatt orbital processing facility as an example. It would hold roughly the processing power of a small commercial server room. But in space it would require 5,640 square meters of deployed solar panels, even in a âdawn-duskâ orbit designed to minimize the time it spends in Earthâs shadow. Thatâs roughly the size of an American football field.

On top of that, the spacecraft would need around 2,500 square meters of radiator panels to stop the electronics from frying themselves. Combining the power generation and cooling equipment required would already bring a spacecraft up to 30 metric tons. Adding in structural trusses, control thrusters, and radiation shielding brings the total mass of 1 MW of orbital data capacity is likely between 34 and 59 metric tons.

For the purposes of practicality, Dr. Turyshev then drops down to a 100 kW center, since a 1 MW data center would not even fit in many modern rocket fairings. Arguably, since each 100 kW data center wouldnât be exactly 10% of the weight of a 1 MW data center, he uses a rough estimate of around 5 metric tons for a single spacecraft of that size. The problem is, to keep up with demand, we would need to launch between 170,000 and 461,000 of them over the course of five years. And each Falcon 9 can only launch at most four of them. That would require almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches over the next five years - or roughly 33 of them per week.

Fraser talks about turning the Moon into a data center.

Even if we had the launch capacity for that sheer scale, there is another bottleneck to contend with - getting the data back to Earth. As we reported earlier this week, weâve made great strides in high-speed optical communications down from orbit lately. However, the headline number of 200 gigabits per second is a single point in time. These âhigh speedâ links realistically deliver around 13 to 26 gigabits per second continuously, in part because they require a direct line of sight to the ground station theyâre communicating with, and they also canât communicate through clouds. Even if we flooded major parts of the Earthâs surface with ground stations, those speeds would severely hobble any interactive cloud apps or data-heavy training runs that require continual syncing with anything on the ground.

But even if we solved the communications problem, thereâs still the problem of that omnipresent menace in space - radiation. Cosmic rays are famous for flipping single bits in computer memory, constantly forcing processors to run error-checking algorithms, and thereby eating into usable computer time. According to the paper, over a five-year mission, the cumulative radiation damage and micrometeoroid impacts would continually degrade both the electronics and solar panels, driving up the cost of every calculation completed.

With all that in mind, the economic hurdle becomes very clear. On Earth, a high-end AI data center costs between $10,000 and $40,000 per kilowatt of computing capacity. In order for a 40-kilogram per kilowatt orbital satellite to match that pricing, it would need combined launch and manufacturing costs of between $250 and $1,000 per kilogram. For comparison, current dedicated Falcon 9 launches work out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram. So the launch cost alone is three to thirteen times more expensive than the entire combined launch and manufacturing cost of a single data center.

Video from Astraveo arguing the same physics as what Dr. Turyshev talks about in the paper. Credit - Astraveo YouTube Channel

With all that said, there are some niche applications for orbital computing in the near future, according to the paper. The first is space-native processing, where satellites crunch the raw imagery for Earth-observation satellites or sensor data before broadcasting high-value insights back down to Earth. Another is communications-based edge computing, where processors piggyback on existing constellations like Starlink that already pay for solar arrays, lasers, and ground stations.

But ultimately, despite this paper, various organizations are moving forward with their plans for data centers in orbit. Even today (November 25th) the FCC approved SpaceXâs application to launch one million âStarmindâ orbital data centers by 2040. Earlier this month, Google booked a flight on a Blue Origin rocket for a test of its Project Suncatcher computing constellation. Until the real economics of the situation catch up with them, it might be a while before these efforts realize what hard physical limits theyâre going up against.

S. G. Turyshev - Orbital Data Centers: Spacecraft Constraints and Economic Viability

#6303. How cranberries went from a Thanksgiving favorite to a symbol of stronger farming for the future

Breeding cultivated cranberries with wild relatives may help protect future crops from extreme heat, frost and climate change.

Cranberries grow in some of the coldest parts of North America, but frost can still damage them.

In spring, frost can damage newly growing buds before they produce berries. In early fall, it can harm fruit that is still ripening.

Scientists crossed cultivated cranberries with a small wild relative from the far north called Vaccinium oxycoccos.

When exposed to cold, these new plants kept more genes involved in growth active than cultivated cranberries did.

The wild plant’s DNA could therefore be of use in breeding cranberries that handle cold weather better.

Audrey Dickinson, a researcher in agricultural genomics at the San Diego Botanic Garden and the Salk Institute, led the study.

Scientists from the USDA’s Agricultural Research Service in Chatsworth, New Jersey, also took part.

Only leaves were sampled, over a span of minutes. Berries and harvests were not included.

The United States is the world’s largest cranberry producer. Strawberries are the only berry Americans eat more of. Most cranberries reach shoppers as juice or as sweetened dried fruit.

Berries can scald once the air passes about 90°F (32°C), and scalded fruit rots more easily. Frost, on the other hand, can leave the fruit soft.

When growers were surveyed, New Jersey producers named heat tolerance first. Wisconsin and British Columbia growers named frost tolerance.

One round of cranberry breeding takes seven to eight years. Most varieties are only a few generations away from wild vines. Wheat breeders, for one, have borrowed heat tolerance from wild relatives.

The small cranberry grows across the cold far north. As its name suggests, its berries are smaller than those of the farmed species.

The two plants look different, but they cross easily. Gene by gene, their published genomes line up closely.

Wild plants for this work were collected in southeastern Alaska in 1996. In 1998, four of them were crossed with the farmed varieties Stevens, Ben Lear and Pilgrim.

For three days, the team kept Stevens and the four hybrid lines at 70°F (21°C). Then the plants went into incubators.

The heated plants reached 117°F (47°C) in 30 minutes, while the chilled plants cooled to 37°F (3°C) over 95 minutes.

The team clipped leaves three times and froze them in liquid nitrogen. Their RNA was read with Oxford Nanopore sequencing, which kept the wild and farmed gene copies apart.

Plants need proteins to grow. Ribosomes assemble those proteins, and the genes that build ribosomes are tied to growth.

Photosynthesis genes, used by leaves to turn sunlight into energy-rich sugars, are tied to growth as well.

Ribosome gene activity declined during the cold test in both Stevens and the hybrids, but the decline was greater in Stevens.

Photosynthesis gene activity increased in the hybrids but decreased in Stevens.

Basic cell work, the researchers suggested, kept going in the hybrids under stress. In Stevens, that work was reduced. Total photosynthesis gene activity, however, stayed higher in Stevens under every condition.

The two groups differed much more in cold than in heat. In the cold test, 18 broad sets of related genes behaved differently between hybrids and Stevens. In the heat test, only one set did.

The team linked this to where the parents come from. The farmed cranberry is native farther south. It may photosynthesize best at warmer temperatures.

A chill that stresses Stevens may be closer to normal growing weather for its wild Alaskan cousin.

The four hybrid lines did not respond in the same way. Gene activity differed more among the lines than between the hybrids as a group and Stevens.

Two lines with the same Stevens parent also differed from each other. The wild parents were therefore likely a major source of this variation.

In the cold test, two lines showed an unusual pattern. At 60 minutes their gene activity shot up. By 95 minutes it had fallen, although the air was still getting colder. In Stevens, large changes continued to the end.

The team sees that rise and fall as a possible sign of efficient adjustment to cold. Results in the heat test were different.

After 30 minutes of heat, Stevens showed the smallest overall change of all the plants.

Some hybrids may cope with cold better than Stevens, then, yet cope with heat worse.

Heat and cold tolerance may need separate tests in breeding programs. Coping with one is no guarantee for the other.

At room temperature, the hybrids mostly took after Stevens. Some 57% of compared genes tracked the farmed parent, against 14% for the Alaskan one.

About 22% of genes were less active in the hybrids than in either parent, many of them tied to photosynthesis. A cold acclimation gene called WCOR413 was among them.

That could hint at hybrid weakness, a known risk when two separately evolved genomes are merged.

Chloroplasts may be part of the explanation. These green structures are where photosynthesis takes place. Many photosynthesis proteins are coded in the cell’s main DNA but work inside chloroplasts.

Chloroplasts also carry a small amount of their own DNA. The two sets of DNA must work together. A mismatch between them could disrupt photosynthesis genes.

To keep the two in step, the authors suggested crossing hybrids back to a farmed cranberry mother several times.

The experiments were short. Only the first 30 minutes of heat and the first 95 minutes of cold were studied. Longer or repeated stress may produce different results.

Gene activity is also only a partial guide to which proteins a plant makes.

The two temperature experiments were also quite different. The heat was intense enough to potentially kill the plants, while the cold temperature was still within the range that cranberries normally experience outdoors.

The researchers also did not measure plant survival, growth or berry production. It is still unclear whether a calmer gene response means a hardier plant.

For Dickinson, the study also highlights why protecting wild plants matters.

“These results highlight the importance of conserving crop wild relatives in their natural habitats and in collections,” she wrote.

Future research could test whether these gene patterns match real frost and heat tolerance in the field.

The study is published in the journal Plants, People, Planet.

#6302. Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A new study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

The characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

The study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

“This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang said.

Aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

Water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

To put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

“This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang said. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”

Reference: “Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling” by Ke Zhang, Yaoyao Han, Lindsey Gillson, Xiaoling Zhang, Suzanne McGowan, Michael E. Meadows, Yuan Jin, Luki Subehi, John A. Dearing, David P. Hamilton, Yan Zhao, Lian Pin Koh and David Taylor, 16 November 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2611874123

“The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene.”

The article doesn’t really support their claim of “increasing synchrony.” This sounds more like assigning a scapegoat than explaining what is driving the alleged changes. It appears to me that the relationship is best described by a U-shaped function rather than a linear, long-term trend. The index graph that is most U-like is the one going back farthest in time, suggesting some periodicity related to time.

The R^2 value in all cases is less than 0.5, and in most cases less than 0.2. That means that the variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the changes in the independent variable is less than the probability of getting a ‘Head’ in a coin flip. That doesn’t convince me that they really understand what is going on. But the buzzword salad had all the right words and conclusions to get published!

#6300. The Event Horizon Telescope Views the Dynamics and Geometry of a Black Hole Jet in Extreme Detail

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jet emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.

Meanwhile, EHT observations in 2021 also resolved the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C 279 in unprecedented detail. These efforts, described in a paper that appeared in Astronomy & Astrophysics, revealed the jet's dynamics and geometry at sub-parsec scales, suggesting it bends toward Earth-based instruments on these scales. Combined with earlier EHT campaigns and multifrequency data, the EHT team's latest results are helping astronomers identify its nature and the mechanisms driving it.

By definition, blazars are bright galaxies with an SMBH at their centers - Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) - that have relativistic jets of ionized matter directed straight toward Earth. Located approximately 538 million light-years away, the jet coming from its center is powered by an SMBH with an estimated mass of about 800 million solar masses (by comparison, Sagittarius A* is about 4.3 million solar masses). Because of its brightness, 3C 279 is considered a prime target for Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) and is frequently used for calibration.

An image of the core region of Messier 87, a supermassive black hole, processed from an array of radio telescopes known as the EHT with colours indicating brightness temperature (Credit: Event Horizon Telescope)

The 2021 campaign represents the largest EHT array configuration published to date, with the addition of two new sites. These were the 12-m telescope at the Kitt Peak Observatory in Arizona and the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) interferometer in the French Alps. These additions provided crucial intermediate baselines that significantly improved coverage, especially at intermediate scales, enabling constraints on specific angular scales. These constraints were essential for probing both compact and extended structures in the jet.

Hendrik MÃ¼ller, a staff scientist in the Data Management and Software (DMS) group at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) and a former researcher with the Max-Planck-Institut fÃ¼r Radioastronomie, was the lead author of the paper that appeared in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. As he told Universe Today via email, the EHT is continuously growing and adding more telescopes every year, including the Greenland Telescope in 2018. But as he noted, the Kitt Peak and NOEMA observatories were especially important to these observations:

The physical baseline between two antennas in the array determines the spatial scale that this baseline can resolve. That is, for example, the reason why the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is built on railway tracks: When you move the antennas closer to each other, you zoom out of the image and see the larger field of view.

If you move them closer to each other, you zoom into the image, achieve higher resolution, but see only a small view of the sky. The locations of the radio telescopes in the EHT could of course not be changed, but Kitt Peak and NOEMA were important because they are relatively close to other telescopes in the array (NOEMA in the French Alpes to Pico Veleta close to Granada, Spain. They added information that was not available to us in previous years.

To process the volumes of data gathered by the EHT arrays, the team relied on Comrade, DoG-HiT, kine, and Difmap imaging software, a strategy similar to the one used to reconstruct the famous M87 black hole image in 2019. As MÃ¼ller explained, the team used different software packages that make different assumptions about the image to build confidence in the result by checking for consistency across methods. Beyond imaging, many more collaborators and software were used during early data-processing steps, like correlation or calibration.

Illustration of the multiwavelength 3C 279 jet structure in April 2017. The observing epochs, arrays, and wavelengths are noted in each panel. Credit: J.Y. Kim/MPIfR/VLBA and GMVA/EHT

The results, as noted, suggest that the jet curves so that one section of it points closer to Earth. While the jet is already oriented towards our instruments, MÃ¼ller explained how this small change can have two visible effects:

Because the plasma is moving close to the speed of light, its radiation is concentrated in the direction it's traveling. When that direction lines up more closely with Earth, we see brighter emission. At the same time, features in the jet are moving more nearly straight toward us, so they can appear to move more slowly across the sky. Think of a car coming almost head-on: it can be moving fast while barely shifting left or right in your field of view.

That's what makes the bend a useful explanation for 3C 279. Farther along the inner jet, we see brighter emission and slower apparent motion. Both can result from a change in direction, even if the plasma keeps moving just as fast. That also means the brightest spot in the image can be downstream from the black hole, where the jet points most directly at us.

What's more, the EHT images show that the direction of the inner jet changes over time, providing clues as to what is driving the jet. From the images, the team also noticed features that appeared to move more slowly along a farther, particularly bright stretch of the jet. The bending towards Earth could explain both effects, as the flow can keep moving just as fast while looking brighter and shifting less laterally. Said MÃ¼ller:

We also found a clue about where the jet picks up speed. Even close to the apparent base of the jet, some features are already moving across the sky at apparent speeds comparable to those much farther downstream. If those features travel with the plasma, that suggests the jet gains much of its speed over a short distance near its base. As the fast flow narrows again, it may form a shock that adds to the brightness we see near the bend.

While 3C 279 is one of the best-studied quasars in radio astronomy, the mechanisms driving its central jet are still a mystery, and future observations could reveal behaviors that have not yet been seen. Astronomers have decades' worth of observations on how its jet behaves on larger scales, but only a few images on how it behaves at the sub-parsec level. Nevertheless, the EHT Collaboration is extremely useful because it enables deep surveys and high resolution, allowing astronomers to detect details in the jet's innermost region that weren't available before. Said MÃ¼ller:

This paper is just the beginning. We have EHT observations from several years, as well as observations at other frequencies that we scheduled around the same time, that are currently [being] analyzed. Observing at different frequencies lets us see different parts of the jet. Taking those observations close together helps us tell which differences come from the frequency we're using and which come from the jet itself changing.

We expect a series of results from these data over the next few years. Very few quasars have been studied in this much detail. That makes 3C 279 one of our best opportunities to understand how a black hole launches a jet and how that jet gets up to nearly the speed of light, and the current manuscript is just the beginning of that journey.

#6299. Losing Weight but Getting Less Healthy? Study Reveals a Dark Side of Keto

Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.

Ketogenic diets have become a popular approach to weight loss, despite conflicting research on their metabolic benefits. A new study in mice suggests that two often overlooked factors may help explain these inconsistencies: the amount of protein in the diet and the genetic makeup of the animals eating it. The findings also raise questions about whether losing weight on a keto diet necessarily means becoming healthier.

The research, published in Cell Metabolism, began when first author Zhaoyue Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow in the Friedman lab, noticed considerable variation in the protein content of ketogenic diets. Although these diets are generally high in fat and extremely low in carbohydrates, their protein content could be contributing to differences in metabolic outcomes.

Zhang and her colleagues systematically tested diets containing different proportions of fat and protein. After four weeks on a ketogenic diet containing just 5% protein, mice belonging to C57Bl/6J, the most commonly used laboratory mouse strain, reduced their food intake by approximately 40% and lost weight. Mice fed an otherwise similar diet containing 10% protein ate more and gained weight. Both groups produced ketones, molecules generated when the body relies heavily on fat for fuel, suggesting that ketosis alone could not account for the difference.

“The result was so striking,” Zhang says.

A closer look at the mice that lost weight revealed a more complicated picture. Although their glucose tolerance, or ability to manage changes in blood sugar, improved, they also developed fatty liver. Much of their weight loss was associated with reductions in lean mass, including muscle.

To understand what was suppressing the animals’ appetite, the researchers investigated GDF15, a hormone released in response to cellular stress that can act on the brain to reduce food intake. When they conducted an experiment using genetically modified mice lacking GDF15, even the control mice unexpectedly failed to lose weight on the low-protein diet.

“At first, I was a bit panicked,” Zhang says. “We had repeated the same experiment many times, and all of a sudden it didn’t work.”

Retracing her steps, Zhang discovered that the genetically modified mice belonged to a different substrain, C57Bl/6N, which shares approximately 99.9% of its genome with the mice used in the earlier experiments.

“This realization was key, and it became the starting point for the rest of the study,” Zhang says.

The researchers eventually identified two genes that helped explain the difference: NNT, which protects cells against oxidative stress, and NLRP12, which helps regulate inflammation. The mice susceptible to weight loss, known as B6J, carried mutations in both genes. Feeding them the low-protein ketogenic diet triggered stress and inflammatory responses in the liver, accompanied by rising levels of GDF15 and an inflammation-associated protein called LCN2. Both proteins can influence appetite through their effects on the brain.

Restoring NNT function in B6J mice caused them to eat more and lose less weight. Conversely, disabling both genes in the genetically similar B6NJ mice, which normally carry functioning versions of both genes, caused them to eat less and lose weight. Treatment with N-acetylcysteine, an antioxidant with anti-inflammatory properties, also lowered circulating levels of GDF15 and LCN2, increased food intake, and reduced weight loss.

Zhang cautions that the findings cannot be directly applied to humans, particularly because the 5% protein diet contained substantially less protein than most ketogenic diets used in clinical trials. Future trials could benefit from paying closer attention to both dietary protein content and genetic differences among participants, while looking beyond weight loss and blood sugar control when assessing metabolic health.

The researchers now want to investigate whether other genetic factors influence responses to ketogenic diets and whether the changes they observed can be reversed once the diet is discontinued.

Reference: “Macronutrient composition and genetic background determine the response to a ketogenic diet in mice” by Zhaoyue Zhang, Alexandre Moura-Assis, Shanshan Liu, Alon Millet, Jordan Shaked, Divya Rajan, Katelin Chen, Anduena Toci, Chloe Schaefer, Ijeoma Obi, Sebastian Carrasco, Sandra Kelly Atkinson, Francois Marchildon, Hanan Alwaseem, Michael Isay-Del Viscio, Henrik Molina, Paul Cohen, Kivanc Birsoy and Jeffrey Friedman, 18 November 2026, Cell Metabolism. DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2026.10.017

#6298. Digital twins of cancer patients could help doctors find better treatments

Digital twins of breast tumors could help doctors predict treatment responses and identify potentially effective alternative drugs.

Ask a chatbot-style AI which drug to give a cancer patient, and it may offer an answer without providing a transparent, scientifically grounded explanation. That, the researchers said, has left many doctors skeptical of such tools.

In London, a team took the opposite route: a program built from logic rather than statistics, which a doctor can open up and read.

Run on virtual copies of 31 real tumors, the program predicted whether a patient’s treatment would work 74% of the time.

For 12 of the 13 patients whose incomplete response the model correctly predicted, it identified at least one additional drug that might have helped.

Jasmin Fisher of the UCL Cancer Institute led the work, with Pedro Victori as first author and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute.

Every result is a simulation checked against records from a trial that has already ended, and the drugs it suggested were not tested in the patients it picked them for.

“We see our computer model as an aid for existing cancer clinical practice, not an alternative to it,” Fisher said.

The cancer in question is triple-negative breast cancer, about 15% of breast cancers.

Its cells lack the three receptors that most breast cancer drugs aim at, so hormone therapies don’t work. About 40% of patients die within five years of diagnosis.

Instead of training on patient data, the team hand-built a map of how the disease works. They read 191 research papers and drew 142 genes, proteins and cell processes as nodes.

Then they linked the nodes with 379 arrows that say which one switches which on or off, and let each node be off, low or fully on.

The map includes the machinery that repairs broken DNA, which chemotherapy and the drug olaparib attack. It also includes the machinery of cell division, which the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel jams.

Two output nodes sum it up: whether the cancer cells die, and whether they keep multiplying.

Before applying the model to individual tumors, the team checked it against 160 laboratory results from 33 other papers and adjusted it until it reproduced all of them.

The patients came from PARTNER, a trial run by Jean Abraham’s team in Cambridge. Its patients, all with triple-negative breast cancer, received four chemotherapy drugs before surgery, with or without olaparib.

For 31 of them, the team had full genome sequences of the tumor.

Each patient’s mutations and missing or duplicated genes were loaded into the map to make a digital twin of the tumor.

A patient with a disabled BRCA1 gene, for instance, had that node fixed at zero. Then the twin was given the same treatment the patient had received, and the program reported whether the cells died.

The predictions matched the real outcomes in 23 of 31 cases. The program was right for 10 of the 14 patients whose cancer disappeared completely, and for 13 of the 17 whose cancer did not.

Only those 23 accurate twins were used for what came next.

The team then took the 13 twins that resisted treatment and switched off every gene in the map, one at a time. They watched for the switch that tipped the simulated cells into dying.

Twelve of the 13 had one. For 10, the program predicted a complete response, eight with a single added drug and two with a pair.

The most broadly useful target was a protein called ATM, which helps cells repair DNA damage; blocking it was predicted to produce a complete response in seven patients.

The other twins pointed to drugs that have passed phase 2 trials, including inhibitors of Chk1, ATR, MEK, mTOR and Wee1.

Fisher said the point is to give a doctor a lead, not an order.

“In practice, the treatment option recommended by our model may, under closer scrutiny, be discounted by the clinician – for example, if they view the drug as too toxic,” she said.

“But it may also lead them to explore, and eventually settle on, a third option which they might otherwise not have arrived at.”

The one tumor for which the program could not identify an effective additional treatment contained three distinct populations of cancer cells.

Spatial RNA data showed three groups of cells with different gene activity sitting in different parts of the tumor.

Simulated separately, each of the three had targets the whole-tumor model had missed. One of them, a lower-grade carcinoma, was predicted to respond completely to an added drug.

A sample taken after treatment held a fourth group unlike any of the first three, carrying two changes the model flags as resistance.

The team also pulled the 29 genes the program had flagged as targets and tested them as a signature in a public database of breast cancer patients.

Among patients with the basal subtype treated with chemotherapy alone, those carrying mutations in the signature genes lived longer.

Thirty-one patients is a small group, and the authors wrote that it limits how finely they can slice the results.

The model is right about three times in four, which also means it is wrong once in four. The twins that failed were set aside before the drug search began.

The map knows only what 191 papers told it, so it can’t propose a mechanism nobody has published.

It also ignores the immune cells and other tissue around a tumor, which matter most for immunotherapy. And it models the drugs used in PARTNER rather than the newer antibody-drug conjugates now in use.

Each twin was built from DNA alone. The authors wrote that adding gene activity and protein data would likely sharpen the predictions.

The framework is designed to be updated as a patient’s tumor changes under treatment.

Determining whether the suggested drugs actually benefit patients will require a clinical trial in which the model’s predictions inform treatment decisions.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Reports Medicine.

#6297. Scientists Uncover a Potential Root Cause of the Global Allergy Epidemic

Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.

Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system. An extensive analysis led by Griffith University researchers challenges decades of conventional thinking about allergic diseases and proposes a potential biological origin for conditions ranging from eczema to food allergies.

The researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function. Their findings suggest that epithelial cells, which form protective barriers along the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus, may struggle to meet environmental and metabolic demands, triggering an excessive immune response.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” said study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist from Griffith’s School of Medicine and Dentistry.

The team examined what it describes as the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data known to the researchers, drawing on 116 case-control cohorts and data from 3,776 patients. Multi-omic analysis combines different types of molecular information to identify biological patterns that might otherwise go undetected.

Scientists may have discovered the hidden cause of allergies. Credit: Professor Peter Smith, Griffith University

“Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces,” Professor Smith said.

“The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow.

“It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions.”

The strongest evidence emerged in eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic inflammatory disease affecting the esophagus. Across all 13 independent patient cohorts, researchers found reduced activity in the cellular process responsible for removing damaged mitochondria.

In patients with eczema, abnormalities affecting the skin’s protective barrier and antioxidant defenses appeared even in areas without inflammation. This finding is consistent with the possibility that cellular dysfunction precedes visible symptoms.

However, the mitochondrial signature was not universal. Researchers found only partial evidence of it in hay fever, while the pattern was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps.

The researchers propose that several environmental factors associated with allergies could converge on the same biological vulnerability: the ability of epithelial cells to generate sufficient energy and withstand stress.

Potential contributors include highly processed diets, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a molecular immunologist from Griffith’s School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences and co-author of the study, said the wide range of factors associated with allergies has made it difficult to develop a unified explanation for their rapid increase within a single generation.

The proposed mechanism could also explain why allergic diseases frequently recur after treatment. Inflammation itself can damage epithelial cells, potentially creating a self-perpetuating cycle of barrier dysfunction and immune activation.

“The research also explains why allergies can relapse,” Associate Professor West said.

“Once inflammation is established it damages the barrier further.

“Today’s drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause.”

The researchers emphasize that their findings support a hypothesis rather than establish a definitive cause of allergies. Direct measurements of epithelial cell function before symptoms appear will be needed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction initiates allergic disease.

“We have spent our careers managing the smoke and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking,” Professor Smith said.

“This is not a cure but is something we have never had before – a logical starting point.

“The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops.”

Reference: “The Origins of Allergy: An Outside-In, Bioenergetic Hypothesis” by Peter K. Smith, Nicholas P. West, Stanley Du Preez, Hugh A. Sampson, Peter W. Hellings, David Price, Liam O’Mahony, Carina Venter, Cezmi A. Akdis and Gil Yosipovitch, 29 October 2026, Allergy. DOI: 10.1111/all.70532

As something of a ‘worse’ but not ‘worst’ case scenario of multiple food and food additive allergies (first documented in late 1981 at age 37) I became mysteriously, seriously ill with chronic fatigue, generalized aches, pains and muscle weakness and serious mood swings in early 1981, following the later learned 1980 FDA approval of the expanded use of added artificially cultured “free” (can cross the blood brain barrier) monosodium glutamate (MSG) as an alleged “flavor enhancer.” All a thorough medical examination revealed was a high blood serum level of uric acid and a low oral temperature (96.8 F, often lower since; metabolic syndrome?). After forty-five years of mostly mild (now) chronic illnesses, medical testing and online research, I’m confident to state that added MSG aggravates (extends and/or intensifies) my basically brief and practically harmless individual allergy reactions to turn them chronic and illness causing. #6296. The Best Little Gifts Your Holiday Party Host Will Actually Want

Don’t show up empty-handed or with a cheap bottle of wine — bring status cocktail cherries, a beeswax candle, or a painterly placemat

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

Even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice company’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

It really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

Swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

When it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

Those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

Is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

#6295. Study Finds Artemis Astronauts Will Enjoy Moon-Grown Potatoes

By now, references to Mark Watney and how he grew potatoes in Martian soil have become a tired clichÃ©. Nevertheless, one can't help but recall the scene whenever news breaks about the latest experiment that examines the potential of growing plants in extraterrestrial soils. The latest comes from Oregon State University (OSU), where researchers have shown that potatoes grown in lunar soil simulant (amended with organic matter) are safe to eat and grow just as well as those produced on Earth.

This is good news for space agencies like NASA that are actively planning to send astronauts back to the Moon, and this time, to stay. Through the Artemis Program, crews will land around the South Pole-Aitken Basin and begin constructing a permanent base that will enable regular missions in the future (about one per year). China's National Space Agency (CNSA) and Roscosmos also plan on building a base - the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) - in the same region by the end of the decade.

To support long-term missions far from Earth, where opportunities for resupply will be fewer and farther between, a degree of self-sufficiency is required. Whereas the International Space Station (ISS) is resupplied regularly and emergency supplies can be dispatched within hours, missions to the Moon will take at least three days to arrive. As such, any sustained program of exploration on the Moon must rely on In-Situ Resource Utilization(ISRU) as much as possible - i.e., using local resources for building materials and providing astronauts with water and food.

Research in the past few decades has led to methods for 3D printing habitats and other facilities using lunar regolith. This can be combined with a bonding agent to create "lunacrete," or sintered with microwaves to create molten ceramic. Either material is then deposited layer by layer by construction robots to form walls and other structural elements. While hydroponics remain a viable way to grow plants (as astronauts do aboard the ISS), the real question is whether Earth plants can be grown in lunar regolith and other extraterrestrial soils.

Led by Aymeric Goyer, a professor with OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, the Oregon team used lunar regolith simulants with different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich organic soil produced when earthworms break down organic matter. With support from NASA's Johnson Space Center Simulant Development Lab, the team produced healthy potatoes with yields comparable to crops grown by farmers in Oregon (the 4th largest potato producer in the U.S.).

Goyer and his teams specifically selected potatoes because they produce more calories per square meter of soil than many other crops. They also offer substantial nutritional value: one medium skin-on potato (148 g/5.3 oz) provides roughly 110 calories, 26 g of carbohydrates, 3 g of protein, and 2 g of fiber. They are also naturally fat-free, gluten-free, cholesterol-free, and are therefore considered a practical staple food for long-duration space missions.

Since lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the researchers tested five simulants representing lunar mare (fine-grained basaltic soil) and lunar highland (feldspar-rich volcanic soil) regions. They also included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, which produces the world's highest potato yield. The results showed that potato plants grown in simulants containing 30% vermicompost grew as well as those cultivated in Earth soils. In other samples, plants grown without vermicompost were severely stunted and had underdeveloped root systems.

The "Moon Village" concept, conceived by MIT in collaboration with the ESA and Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. Credit: ESA/Skidmore, Owings & Merrill

Lastly, those grown with 5% to 15% vermicompost showed only partial growth. As Goyer said in an OSU press release:

We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter. That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.

The results also showed that the potatoes grown in lunar regolith simulants maintained their nutritional quality, with no statistically significant increase in naturally occurring potato toxins (glycoalkaloids) often associated with green discoloration. Lunar regolith still presents many challenges for plant growth, which include extremely fine-grained dust and elevated levels of heavy metals.

But the researchers are confident that adding organic matter helps bind heavy metals, preventing them from damaging roots, interfering with growth, or leaching into the potatoes themselves. In the future, astronauts could bring compost to the Moon, along with Earth worms, to create their own fertilizer, augmenting soil collected during surface trips to grow their food.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," said David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab. Their results are reported in a paper, "Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants," that appeared in npj Microgravity. Another paper, which reports the results of experiments involving 10 potato varieties to identify which grow best in lunar soil, will be released.

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon.
