#6281. An overlooked brain region offers new clues to how memory works

In mice, a thin brain sheet called the claustrum kept a smell or a touch in working memory for 30 seconds, and quieting it cut performance.

Anyone following a conversation holds the last sentence in mind while the next one arrives. The sound is gone within a moment, yet the brain keeps using it for seconds, and where it keeps it is only partly understood.

Part of that job, at least in mice, belongs to a sliver of nerve cells wedged between the cortex and the structures beneath it.

The sliver is called the claustrum. In mice, it kept a trace of a smell or a touch for up to 30 seconds. Quieting it cut the animals’ scores on a memory task by roughly 40% to 60%.

Alan Carleton and Ivan Rodriguez of the University of Geneva led the work, with Anindya Bhattacharjee as first author.

Carleton’s lab in the Department of Basic Neurosciences studies how the brain handles the senses, and the claustrum caught the team’s attention because of its wiring.

“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” Carleton said.

The short-term hold the study tested is called working memory. Reading and deciding both depend on it, and it is impaired in disorders such as schizophrenia and ADHD.

It runs on brain circuits spread across many regions, and how those circuits hold information over time isn’t clear.

The team trained head-fixed mice on a game of same or different.

A tone marked the start of each trial. Then came a one-second cue. It was one of two odors, or a puff of air on the left or right whiskers.

After a delay of 5 to 60 seconds, a second cue arrived. If it differed from the first, the mouse earned a drop of water by licking a tube. If it matched, licking earned nothing.

Thirty mice learned the odor version, and within about 400 trials they were scoring above 70%. Twenty-three of the 25 mice given the whisker version learned it too.

Scores fell as the delay grew. The memory faded at the same rate for both senses, with a half-life of about 20 seconds in the typical mouse.

In seven mice, the team watched claustrum cells through a tiny lens while the animals played. Each cell carried a sensor that glows when the cell is active.

About a quarter of the cells fired at the cue, and about 60% fired during the wait. Roughly a quarter responded to one cue but not the other.

The cells’ activity shifted as the wait went on. Even so, a computer program reading the whole population could still tell which cue the mouse had received, right up to the second cue, at every delay tested.

On trials the mouse got wrong, the program did far worse.

“Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time,” Rodriguez said. “Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”

Only a small share of the cells tracked licking or movements of the nose, mouth or forepaw, about 8% at most for any one of them.

The findings suggest that the memory trace was not simply a reflection of the animal’s movements.

To test whether the claustrum was needed, the team dialed its cells down in two ways. A drug that acts only on cells carrying an engineered receptor cut scores by about 40%.

Optogenetics, in which cells carry a light-sensitive protein and a fiber delivers light for about one second, cut them by 40% to 60%.

The light trials were mixed in with ordinary trials in the same session, and performance suffered regardless of when the light was delivered.

Dimming the claustrum during the first cue, early in the wait, late in the wait or during the second cue hurt in every case.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” Carleton said.

Mice carrying a harmless protein instead of the light-sensitive one played as well with the light on as off.

The same mice then played a version with no delay, telling two odors or two puffs apart on the spot. The light had no effect on that.

The mice’s pupils, body movements and licking looked the same with and without it, and they didn’t lick early during long waits. What fell was the rate of correct licks on trials where the cues differed.

“Disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself,” Carleton said.

The sliver is thin and poorly bounded, so the team could only partly quiet it, and the mice still scored well above chance. Other regions carry short-term memories too, and this study doesn’t say how the work is shared.

A second team reported in June on a set of cells in and around the claustrum that connect to the prefrontal cortex. Mice needed those cells while holding a location in mind in a maze.

Silencing them during the decision itself improved performance, the opposite of what the Geneva team saw.

The two groups used different tasks and targeted different cells, and neither result settles which cells do what.

How the claustrum keeps a memory steady while its own activity drifts is the open question.

The next step, Carleton said, is to work out how the claustrum talks to the cortex, and how that exchange keeps a held memory from degrading.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6279. Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space. JPl physicist Dr. Slava Turyshev, who wrote the paper at the center of that article, also published a follow-up study in August, available in preprint on arXiv, about how getting the hardware off the ground is only half the battle. Once all that equipment is up there, someone, or something, is going to have to maintain it.

Modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem. The computer chips and memory that power AI data centers become obsolete every 3-5 years. If a company builds an orbital data center, its processing power is effectively useless for training the latest AI models in less than half a decade. So, in their business plans, the solution is to build intentionally disposable satellites.

Unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware. Given that those bulkier pieces of equipment pose their own challenge for launches, as we saw yesterday, that seems a bit of a waste. So, Dr. Turyshev suggests that orbital data centers must be designed with hardware replacement in mind.

Fraser talks about a NASA project designed to assemble large-scale structures in space.

On Earth, replacement of data server racks involves a human technician walking down an air-conditioned aisle, pulling some cables, and pressing pins before replacing a standardized blade. In orbit, that would require a pressurized housing with airlocks, life support and fire suppression systems, while still having the problem of cooling all of those heat-producing microchips in the vacuum of space. According to Dr. Turyshev, that means the entire data center architecture should be based around plug-and-play âorbital replacement unitsâ (ORUs).

He assigns each of those ORUs into one of three main replaceable component tiers (alongside replacing an entire 100 kW satellite node if it suffers catastrophic damage). One is a 5 kW âcomputeâ module that holds the memory, storage and optical transceivers necessary to actually perform calculations. These are designed to be rapidly swappable, and are intended to be the most replaced part of the whole satellite.

Another ORU category is the âsubsystemsâ â the power converters, batteries, pumps, and manifolds meant to keep the whole system running but that are settled enough technologically to not require regular replacement. In the paperâs architecture, these can be swapped out by specialized 6 or 7 degree-of-freedom robotic arms, as compared to the automated cartridge changers that handle replacing the compute modules.

Fraser talks about the difficulties repairing missions at L2, like JWST.

The third group of ORUs consists of the solar arrays and radiator panels themselves. Making them modular has the added advantage of not needing to replace the entire cooling or power generation system if one part happens to be struck by a micrometeoroid, which will undoubtedly happen often even in Low Earth Orbit. Despite the fact these modules make up the bulk of the weight and surface area of the spacecraft, they will not have to be repaired as frequently as the compute modules, as random failures caused by cosmic rays will brick compute modules fairly frequently..

Unfortunately, replacing these systems isnât as easy as it would be on Earth. Each 5 kW processor will heat up nearly half a degree Celsius every second, triggering a thermal overload in a little less than a minute if left uncooled. And the power capacitors riding along to maintain power to the system have the capability of producing an arc strong enough to weld a robotic gripper to a maintenance touch point, so they must be bled off before a robot can start interacting with the satelliteâs hardware.

And then, there is once again the sense of scale. For a standardized 1 MW cluster, comprising ten 100 kW sized systems, a collection of 3-4 robots specialized assigned to each 1MW cluster would have to perform around four hundred standardized swaps per year â more than one a day. This would include replacing broken or damaged parts, as well as upgrading to the server hardware itself.

Hubble has already been repaired by a crewed mission. NASA wants to do it again, Great Space expliains. Credit - Great Space YouTube Channel

Scaling that up once again to a 1 GW computer cluster, comparable to a major modern AI campus here on Earth, the number becomes staggering. There would have to be 400,000 automated replacement tasks every year. And supplying the parts to do that would require launching up to 25 metric tons of replacement cargo every day.

To put it bluntly, we donât have that kind of launch capacity yet. Nor would sending humans up help manage such a drastic workload. The paper estimates that housing and feeding a crew of 4-6 technicians to actively manage a data center constellation would require $500 million to $1.5 billion per year. Until we get to the scale of several hundred megawatts to a gigawatt-level system, that is not economically feasible.

Thatâs not to say we couldnât launch specialized crewed repair missions occasionally. But at the scales needed to make a dent in the AI infrastructure we have down here on Earth, it would be hard to keep up with the overall maintenance workload using humans. And unfortunately, the entire concept of maintenance is another area that the back-of-the-envelope calculations of the companies that want to build orbital data centers seem to ignore.

Their solution is simply to add some extra hardware to account for the inevitable damage/failure that comes with operating in space. While that might work for a little while, if the plan is to have a long-term data center presence in orbit, it's better to design for at least the possibility of continual operation rather than burning up tens of thousands of satellites in fireballs across the world every year. It remains to be seen if that message will get across to the people designing these systems, though.

S. G. Turyshev - Operations, Maintenance, and Industrial Scaling of MW-Class Orbital Data Centers

UT - The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

#6278. Scientists Successfully Grow Potatoes in Simulated Moon Soil

Successful potato harvests in simulated lunar soil suggest that future astronauts could recycle their food scraps to help grow their next meal.

A future in which humans live on the Moon and grow their own food may be a little closer to reality thanks to one of Earth’s most familiar crops. Researchers at Oregon State University have successfully grown edible potatoes in simulated lunar soil, achieving growth and yields comparable to those produced on Earth by adding compost made with the help of earthworms.

The findings support NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon. Producing food locally would reduce dependence on costly resupply missions from Earth and help make long-term lunar exploration more sustainable. Potatoes are particularly appealing because they provide substantial nutritional value and produce more calories per unit of land than many other crops.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” said Aymeric Goyer of Oregon State University’s Department of Botany and Plant Pathology. “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”

One of the biggest agricultural challenges on the Moon lies directly beneath astronauts’ feet. Most of the lunar surface is covered in regolith, a layer of loose rock and dust containing very little organic matter.

In a study published in npj Microgravity, Goyer and his colleagues tested whether adding different amounts of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich material produced when earthworms break down organic matter, could make simulated lunar soil suitable for growing potatoes.

Because the composition of lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the team tested five simulants representing both the Moon’s darker plains, known as lunar maria, and its highland regions. For comparison, they included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for producing some of the highest potato yields in the world.

Potato plants grown in simulated lunar soil without compost were severely stunted and developed poorly formed roots. Adding between 5% and 15% vermicompost led to only partial recovery. However, plants grown with 30% vermicompost matched the growth and development of those cultivated in Earth soils.

Lunar regolith also contains elevated levels of heavy metals that can damage plant roots and interfere with growth.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds,” said David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer’s lab.

The researchers suspect that organic matter binds to heavy metals, making them less available to plants and limiting their harmful effects.

Growing potatoes successfully would mean little if astronauts could not safely eat them. Encouragingly, potatoes produced in the lunar soil simulants maintained their nutritional quality and showed no statistically significant increase in glycoalkaloids, naturally occurring potato toxins often associated with green discoloration beneath the skin. The findings indicate that the potatoes were safe to eat under the conditions tested.

Future lunar explorers could potentially bring a small supply of organic matter from Earth and gradually produce more by recycling food scraps and plant waste. Such a system could turn everyday waste into valuable growing material while reducing the supplies astronauts would need to transport from Earth.

The research team is now investigating which potatoes might be best suited for lunar agriculture. A forthcoming paper will report results from experiments involving 10 potato varieties grown in simulated lunar soil.

Reference: “Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants” by David Handy, Anika Loeffler, Medora Knudson, Sydney Campbell, Pankaj Jaiswal, Jeffrey C. Anderson and Aymeric Goyer, 19 November 2026, npj Microgravity. DOI: 10.1038/s41526-026-00668-z

#6277. Violent star collisions may have created the earliest giant black holes

Crowded early star clusters could merge stars into one giant, and a new model shows how that giant may become a black hole seed.

Space is so empty that two stars almost never hit each other. In the first star clusters, though, stars were packed so tightly that they may have crashed into one another again and again.

A new model suggests those crashes could merge stars until one carried the mass of the whole cluster. A star that heavy may have no way to die except by collapsing into a black hole.

That matters because the James Webb Space Telescope keeps finding enormous black holes far earlier in cosmic history than astronomers expected.

The new work, led by Claire Williams, a doctoral student at UCLA, is a calculation rather than an observation. It maps where colliding stars could have made the seeds of those black holes.

Webb’s deep images show extremely compact star clusters in the early universe, and computer simulations of that era produce the same crowding.

Williams and her colleagues in the UCLA Division of Astronomy and Astrophysics built a model to ask what happens to the stars inside them.

Co-authors of the study came from Northwestern’s CIERA and seven other institutions.

The model clusters ranged from about two-thirds of a light-year in radius to roughly 300 light-years.

They held anywhere from ten thousand to a billion times the mass of the Sun. Some had a black hole at the center and some did not.

For each one, the team worked out how often stars would run into each other before something stopped them. That could be the stars burning out or a neighboring clump of matter crashing in.

Even with the strictest assumptions, collisions should have been common in many of these systems. Test simulations tracking 1,000 individual stars near a cluster’s center agreed on where they happen.

In an interview with Earth.com, Williams said star collisions matter today only in rare, extreme places, such as the cores of galaxies. So astronomers usually don’t treat them as central to how stars live.

“We were surprised to discover how ubiquitous these collisions might have been,” she said.

What a collision does depends on how fast the two stars meet. If they meet at speeds below the escape speed at a star’s surface, they can merge into one bigger star.

At higher speeds, collisions can strip material from both stars or destroy them entirely, releasing gas from their interiors.

In a cluster with no black hole, the model found no system where stars moved fast enough to destroy each other. Every collision was a merger.

And because the merged stars are heavier than their neighbors, they sink toward the center quickly, where they collide again.

“Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster,” Williams said.

“When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole.”

How big that merged star gets depends mostly on how tightly the cluster is packed.

In the model’s standard setup, the central star passes 200 times the Sun’s mass only once a cluster holds roughly 100,000 suns’ worth of stars per cubic parsec. A parsec is about 3.3 light-years.

Above that line, nearly all of the lightest clusters in the model produced one. In the densest cases, the merged star passed 100,000 solar masses.

When the team filled the clusters with heavy stars instead of Sun-like ones, only 22 systems built a giant at all, and the largest reached 512 solar masses. Heavy stars burn out quickly, so the collisions ran out of time.

If each giant collapses into a black hole of the same mass, the result is an intermediate-mass black hole, a size astronomers have struggled to find.

Other groups have already proposed stellar mergers as a route to early black holes, and the team’s giant-star masses broadly agree with theirs.

The new part is one framework that runs from an ordinary early cluster to a black hole star wrapped in gas.

Once a black hole is at the center, the outcome changes. Its gravity speeds up the stars closest to it, so collisions there happen too fast to merge.

The stars are torn apart instead, and the gas from their interiors piles up in a tiny region around the black hole.

The Milky Way’s center is the nearby example. “One place in the nearby universe where collisions between stars are common is the galactic center,” Williams said.

“In our model, once these very massive stars turn into intermediate-mass black holes, the system resembles our own galactic center, which is a black hole surrounded by a dense star cluster.”

That dense, gassy core is why the authors connect the model to Webb’s little red dots.

Astronomers believe these compact objects hold a rapidly growing black hole, and several recent studies describe that black hole as buried in dense gas.

In the model, a cluster as dense as a little red dot would build a central star of 10,000 to 100,000 solar masses. Once a black hole formed, collisions would keep feeding gas toward it.

Williams said other researchers had already proposed that very massive stars might be connected to the dots.

“Little Red Dots may represent the densest extreme of a continuum of stellar systems that formed naturally in the early Universe, rather than an entirely separate class of object,” she told Earth.com.

Smadar Naoz, a UCLA astrophysicist and co-author, compared the research on the dots to the tale of blind people each describing an elephant by the part they touch.

“Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant,” Naoz said.

Asked by Earth.com what Webb could see to confirm the picture, Williams said there may not be a single “smoking gun.”

The most direct test, she said, is spectroscopy, which splits an object’s light into its component wavelengths.

The bright and dark lines in that spectrum reveal the temperature, chemical makeup and motion of the material giving off the light.

With better theoretical predictions, those lines could help tell light from very massive stars apart from light reworked by gas around a black hole that is actively feeding.

One clue would be unusual amounts of certain elements, thrown out when collisions expose the insides of stars. The gas from these collisions may be unusually rich in nitrogen, which has already turned up in some early clusters.

A second test would look for leftovers. If collisions built very massive stars that later collapsed, some of the resulting black holes may now wander near the edges of galaxies.

In a newer preprint that has not been peer reviewed, Williams’s team reports that upcoming sky surveys could find them.

Surveys by the Rubin Observatory and the Roman Space Telescope may spot the black holes when they destroy stars that pass too close.

“Finding a larger population of these events would provide independent evidence that dense early clusters formed intermediate-mass black holes through runaway stellar collisions,” Williams said.

The authors list what their simplified model leaves out. It ignores any gas left over from the cluster’s birth, which they expect would pull merged stars inward even faster.

It doesn’t update the stars’ masses as mergers happen, so it may miss runaway growth.

Its estimate of how much material a fast collision strips from a star is also likely too high. So the gas densities around black holes may be overstated.

The model also stops at the giant star. It doesn’t follow whether that star collapses, how much of its mass ends up inside a black hole, or how fast the black hole grows afterward.

Williams said the team’s next step is following the gas that fast collisions throw into the middle of a cluster. The current model estimates how much gas that makes, but not where it goes.

The gas could stay trapped, cool and feed the black hole, change the orbits of nearby stars, or be driven out. Each outcome would leave a different signature for telescopes to look for.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal.

#6276. 2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality

At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best New Restaurants in America.

The Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best New Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

The Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” says Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside big coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”

One of those chefs who left New York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he says. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”

It’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey says they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”

At Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he says. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”

That welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it shows that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall says. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”

#6275. Three Ancient Cosmic Collisions May Explain Why the Moon Has Two Faces

Scientists have narrowed down when three massive collisions reshaped the Moon, bringing them closer to understanding why its Earth-facing side looks so different from its far side.

Billions of years ago, a collision powerful enough to melt enormous quantities of lunar rock created the Moon’s largest impact basin. Subsequent collisions broke apart and scattered some of that ancient material across the surface, leaving behind a geological record that scientists are now piecing together.

Located on the Moon’s far side, the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the oldest and largest impact structures in the solar system. Understanding its history could help explain why the Moon’s near and far sides are so different, what lies beneath its surface, and when major collisions occurred during its early evolution.

An international research team led by Professor Guochun Zhao, Mok Sau-King, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), and Dr. Yuqi Qian, the study’s first author, has identified two types of magnesium-rich rocks with remarkably different origins. Published in Science Advances, the research also establishes a clearer timeline of the major impacts that shaped the region.

For decades, the basin remained largely unexplored. That changed in 2019, when Chang’e-4 completed the first successful landing on the Moon’s far side, followed in 2024 by Chang’e-6, which brought the first rock samples from this largely unexplored region back to Earth.

Using Chang’e-6 samples allocated to HKU DEPS and surface measurements from both missions, the researchers obtained the first direct geological evidence from the two landing sites for reconstructing the basin’s impact history. Satellite observations and numerical simulations helped them trace the origins of rocks across the wider basin.

One group of rocks, known as moderately magnesium-rich norites, formed in the aftermath of the original SPA collision. The impact generated a thick sheet of molten rock that gradually cooled, with different minerals crystallizing at different stages. Later collisions exposed these ancient rocks at the central peaks of large craters. Some were eventually blasted toward the Chang’e-4 landing site in Von Kármán crater by the impact that formed Finsen crater.

The second group contained considerably more magnesium and likely formed through a separate process called magnesium-suite magmatism, a type of magma activity associated with the original SPA impact. These rocks were exposed along the western ring of mountain peaks within the Apollo basin before the Chaffee S impact scattered some of them toward the Chang’e-6 landing site.

Earlier research by the HKU-led team had already uncovered evidence of prolonged volcanic activity and previously unrecognized magma activity in the region. Those studies also suggested that underground accumulations of titanium-rich minerals, known as ilmenite-bearing cumulates, helped account for the contrasting volcanic histories of the Moon’s two sides.

The latest findings suggest that the South Pole-Aitken basin formed approximately 4.34 billion years ago. Another major collision created the Apollo basin around 4.2 billion years ago, followed by the formation of the Orientale basin approximately 3.87 billion years ago. Together, these three events reveal how successive collisions reshaped the Moon’s largest impact basin over hundreds of millions of years.

Reference: “Postimpact evolution of the South Pole–Aitken basin revealed by Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6” by Yuqi Qian, Wenlei Song, James Head, Mingyu Tian, Zhuang Guo, Harald Hiesinger, Carolyn H. van der Bogert, Le Zhang, Jingyou Chen, Wanfeng Zhang, Ziqing Li, Lingzhi Sun, Xiangsong Wang, Wei-Ran Li, Jiacheng Liu, Nicolas Dauphas, Yi-Gang Xu and Guochun Zhao, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh9798

#6274. Detection of Vaporized Rock Reveals the Birth of a Solar System

Astronomers have detected titanium oxide in gas form for the first time around a young, massive star. The detection offers a rare glimpse into the very earliest stages of solar system formation, before the formation of planets and asteroids.

The detection was made around a young protostar called Orion Source I, which lies some 1500 light-years from Earth. Orion Source I has not yet reached the main sequence phase of a starâs life cycle â it continues to accrete material from its surrounding molecular cloud.

Models of solar system formation have long held that certain rocky molecules, ones which are stable at high temperatures, act as the âseedsâ that make up the dust in a protoplanetary disk, and later form the basis for rocky planets like Earth and Mars. This includes elements like calcium, aluminum, and titanium. Only later do materials that vaporize easily â volatiles like water, for example â accrete to young solar system objects.

But itâs not exactly clear where these seeds form. Samples collected from our own solar system suggest that they form under high-temperature conditions. They are, as far as we can tell, the oldest solids ever formed in our solar system.

Now, for the first time, this detection of titanium oxide around Orion Source I is providing astronomers more direct evidence of vaporized rock at the dawn of a new star system.

âWe're in a unique situation with this object, Orion Source I,â said Adam Ginsburg, Associate Professor at the University of Florida and a co-author on the paper announcing the discovery. âThis object has a luminous enough star that it's evaporating the rock. We're seeing the rock evaporate from solid into gas, and so we can do the spectroscopy now and figure out what the rock is made of.â

Ginsberg and his coauthors are getting the first real glimpses at the formation environments of these rocky dust-seeding materials, which complements knowledge gathered from our own solar system.

âThe exciting thing is we're seeing the titanium oxide; we can measure how much there is, and we can start comparing our measurements to how our own solar system formed,â Ginsburg said. âIn our solar system, we can measure the ratios between different types of rocks, different elements, because we can grab those rocks and bring them into a lab.â

This isnât the first time Orion Source I has provided valuable insights into solar system formation. In 2019, salty compounds were similarly detected in the protoplanetary disk.

While the salt was found mainly in the outer disk around the star, the titanium oxide was found closer in, at the base of the starâs outflow of material: a hotter, more extreme region where the material could be vaporized. Understanding the origin of this material is an important discovery for researchers trying to piece together exactly how a new solar system comes together, and offers a glimpse into the past of our own star and rocky neighbourhood.

The detection was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2026.

Scott Johnston is a science communicator and author with a PhD in the history of science. He is the author of an academic book, âThe Clocks are Telling Lies,â that explores the history of global timekeeping, and is a senior science writer at Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics.

#6273. An elusive porcupine has a hidden glow that scientists just discovered

Researchers discovered that Mexican hairy dwarf porcupines glow under ultraviolet light, making them easier to spot at night.

The Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine is difficult to see in a tree even during the day. When ultraviolet light is shone on one at night, however, its quills glow a blue-green color.

This glow was observed on every live porcupine examined by a research team in southeastern Mexico. The researchers also used it to locate the animals in the treetops after dark.

Living animals also glowed far more brightly than old skins kept in a museum.

The team wrote that “no photoluminescence observations have ever been made in live individuals of the Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine.”

The study was carried out at El Colegio de la Frontera Sur (ECOSUR) in Chetumal, Quintana Roo.

Since 2023 the institution has helped environmental authorities to rescue and examine porcupines living in the city.

The Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine is a small spiny rodent that lives alone and is active at night. It spends most of its life in trees.

The species belongs to the same family as the larger North American porcupine. It is found from central Mexico to Panama, but little is known about its basic habits.

The first observation was made in June 2024 by senior author Jonathan Pérez-Flores. He was examining two females when he pointed a small ultraviolet flashlight at them and their quills lit up.

Ultraviolet light lies just beyond violet at the edge of human vision. Some materials absorb this light and release it again as a color that people can see.

The effect is known as photoluminescence. A similar thing happens when a white T-shirt is placed under a blacklight.

The flashlight used by the team also produced some visible purple light. For that reason only other colors such as green, blue and yellow were treated as a true glow.

Twenty adult porcupines were examined over the following three months. Seventeen of these animals were female and three were male.

Each porcupine was sedated for a health check. While it recovered in a quiet and dark place the light was held about a foot (30 centimeters) away.

Most of the photographs were taken with ordinary mobile phones.

All 20 animals glowed and this was true for both males and females. The head was the brightest region and showed a greenish-blue color.

The head also carries more quills than any other part of the body. The back, the legs and the tail showed the same greenish-blue wherever quills were present.

On the belly the glow varied in strength, which the team linked to the wider spacing of its quills.

Freshly collected quills told a more detailed story. Each one showed green where it looks yellow in daylight and blue at its brown tip.

Patches of skin without hair or quills did nothing more than reflect the purple of the flashlight. Neither the hair nor the claws glowed in any of the 20 animals.

The most unusual result came from the hands and feet of the porcupines. The palms and the soles of the feet produced a bright yellow glow that was visible from a distance.

“To the best of our knowledge, this phenomenon has not been reported in any other species of mammal,” the authors wrote. A 2023 catalog of 125 glowing mammals contains no such pattern, they noted.

Glowing has been described in a growing number of mammals, including domestic cats, pocket gophers and North American bats.

The source of the yellow glow on the palms and soles has not been identified.

The researchers suspect that pigments or proteins in that skin are involved but these were not tested in the study.

Two preserved porcupines from the ECOSUR museum collection were examined in the same way for comparison. Both specimens had been prepared more than 10 years earlier without the use of fluorescent chemicals.

In ordinary light the quills of these specimens had a pale cream color. Under ultraviolet light they gave off a greenish glow so faint that it could barely be seen.

No glow at all was observed on the skin or fur of the museum specimens. The palms and soles that had shone so brightly on the living animals also remained dark.

The authors suspect that the age of the specimens explains much of the gap. Keratin, the main material in quills as well as in human hair and nails, degrades slowly as the years pass.

Light could have made matters worse, since it destroys glowing molecules in keratin through a process called photobleaching.

This finding is relevant because the majority of studies on glowing mammals have relied on museum specimens.

Porcupines have been included in only a few of these studies and observations of live animals had been anecdotal.

The authors argued that “it is essential to conduct this type of research on both living and dead organisms to observe any differences.”

The authors cited a 2022 study that found green-glowing quills on museum skins of African porcupines but not American ones.

The researchers next wanted to know whether the glow had practical value, since canopy animals are hard to census.

For the test they chose trails on the ECOSUR campus where porcupines had been seen before. The route was walked twice a month from July to December 2024.

Every walk began no earlier than 7 p.m. and ended by midnight along roughly 0.6 mile (1 kilometer) of trail. At 10 stops spaced about 330 feet (100 meters) apart, the canopy was searched for 15 minutes.

Trees along the route stood 39 to 49 feet (12 to 15 meters) tall. Even so, the quills and soles stood out against leaves, bark and fungi.

Over the 12 walks, porcupines were detected 20 times, or roughly 1.7 sightings per route.

This porcupine is docile and can stay still for several minutes, so the animals found were photographed and filmed.

The authors wrote that “no previous study had used this method for locating arboreal mammals during nighttime surveys.”

The survey method does have an important limitation. Males and females of this species cannot easily be distinguished and individual animals lack any markings that would identify them.

For this reason the 20 sightings may not represent 20 different porcupines. The same animal could have been recorded on more than one night.

The photographs were also taken in a range of settings and mostly with mobile phones. Only three of the 20 sedated porcupines were male.

The function of glowing in mammals remains a matter of debate among scientists. Some researchers consider it a simple by-product of the pigments or structure of fur and skin.

Others prefer a checklist of five criteria drawn up by earlier researchers. Under it the glowing material should sit somewhere visible.

The animal should also live in conditions where the glow would show.

A third criterion asks for visual behaviors that might rely on the pattern. The remaining two deal with the wavelengths involved and with whether any onlooker has eyes sensitive to them.

In the porcupine’s case the authors believe the first three have been met. A related species, Coendou spinosus, presents its back and vibrates its quills when threatened. A glow could add to that display.

“Photoluminescent structures may facilitate perception and communication among individuals of this species during the night,” the authors wrote.

For the other two criteria the evidence is circumstantial. Many rodents may see ultraviolet light. Nobody has checked this porcupine for the light-sensing proteins, called opsins, that this would need.

Future research could test whether porcupines use the glow to find one another in the dark.

The flashlight used in the study emitted light at 395 nanometers and this appears strongly violet.

The team recommends that surveys also test ultraviolet light at a shorter wavelength of 365 nanometers, since some animals glow differently under each wavelength.

The study shows that a simple flashlight can help scientists find an animal that is otherwise very difficult to observe.

The full study was published in the journal Neotropical Biology and Conservation.

#6272. Experimental Drug Shrinks Tumors in Two of the Hardest-To-Treat Cancers

A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.

When pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options. In some patients, the difficulty lies in genetic mutations that keep cancer cells growing and have historically been difficult to target with drugs. An experimental cancer drug called ERAS-0015 has shown promising results in an early clinical trial, shrinking tumors in patients who had already undergone other forms of treatment.

The drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division. In healthy cells, RAS proteins act like molecular switches, turning on when cells receive signals to grow and turning off when those signals are no longer needed. Certain genetic mutations can leave these switches stuck in the “on” position, continuously instructing cells to grow and helping sustain cancer.

For years, scientists struggled to develop drugs capable of interfering with these faulty proteins. ERAS-0015 takes an approach known as a pan-RAS molecular glue. It works by bringing proteins together at the molecular level and is designed to bind to RAS while the switch is active, blocking growth signals associated with several different cancer-driving RAS mutations.

“The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient’s mutation, or the ‘Achilles Heel’ of a specific individual’s cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations,” said Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute in Sarasota, Florida.

Wang presented findings from 148 patients participating in the phase I AURORAS-1 clinical trial on November 19, 2026, at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

The trial began in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 both alone and in combination with other anticancer therapies. Participants include people with pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread beyond the original tumor site, and other solid tumors driven by RAS mutations. The results presented at the symposium included 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC. The trial is continuing to enroll patients.

“AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients that have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer. A ‘response’ means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are important as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer. In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects,” Wang told the symposium.

These response rates came from relatively small groups of patients receiving a 32 mg dose of the drug. Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients with pancreatic cancer who had previously received chemotherapy and in three of five patients with lung cancer who had previously been treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, drugs that help the immune system recognize and attack cancer, or platinum-based chemotherapy.

Researchers gradually increased doses of ERAS-0015 from 2 mg to 40 mg to evaluate how well patients tolerated the drug. After a median follow-up of just over four months, there was no indication that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

At doses of 16 to 32 mg, the most common side effects, affecting at least 10% of patients, were rash, diarrhea, nausea, and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) experienced severe treatment-related side effects, classified as grade 3 or higher. No dose-limiting side effects were reported.

“We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients that have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer,” said Wang.

“Our goal is to give clinicians new, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options.”

Phase I clinical trials involve relatively small numbers of patients and are primarily designed to evaluate safety and determine appropriate doses. Although the tumor shrinkage observed in this trial provides an early indication of the drug’s potential, larger phase II and phase III clinical trials will be necessary to confirm its safety and effectiveness.

“If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a new option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1,” Wang concluded.

Professor Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology’s clinical research program, was not involved in the study. She commented: “This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging anti-tumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

“This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently.”

#6271. The Best Fancy Food Gifts (That We Actually Want for Ourselves)

These Japanese toaster ovens, sleek barware sets, and design-forward coffee grinders will bring a lifetime of (tasty) memories

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Forgive the Daddy Warbucks-ness of what I’m about to say, but I think it’s important to remember that a splurge and an extravagance aren’t quite the same thing when it comes to gifts. On one end of the spectrum, there are vapid luxury items; on the other, there are the gifts whose steeper price point is tied directly to their artistry, quality, and/or durability. While the former can be fun to window-shop, our hard-earned clams are best spent on the latter.

As a seasoned shopping writer, I ask myself two big questions when mulling over a pricey purchase: What is the story behind this item? Can I picture it in my life for years to come?

Consider the iconic, mid-century modern Moccamaster coffee machine, which first debuted in the 1960s and has been trending on social media lately for its array of colorful, modular designs. I took the cult-fave machine for an extended test run (it’s still my daily driver), and the yellow pepper iteration made me fall in love with drip coffee all over again. The Dutch company behind the appliance, Technivorm, really exercises what it calls its core tenets of “form and function,” and will service any repairs on the machines for up to five years. That is exactly the kind of lore I crave from the splurge-level items on my holiday shopping list (and the kind that will make your own design-savvy, coffee-loving giftee feel special).

If you’re reaching into your budget for gifts that last, impress, and — if you’re giving them to a family member or partner — you might be able to use yourself for years to come, the fancy gifts for food lovers start getting good. There are the big-ticket kitchen titans: a high-tech Mill food recycler, sleek Miele vacuums (post-kitchen-prep cleanup doesn’t stand a chance), and electric pizza ovens that can reach 850 degrees Fahrenheit in just 90 seconds. Sometimes “splurges” are just wise investments, especially with appliances and cookware; your giftee is going to use a well-made cutting board or top-tier kitchen knife for years or decades to come. There are also the gifts with spectacular whimsy: a stationary exercise bike that makes smoothies, a martini-lover’s menorah, a tabletop lighter that’s also an incredible conversation piece.

These gifts may be at higher price points than a classic stocking stuffer, but they’re also extra-special — we’d say, so worth it if you have the dough. If you’re looking to roll out the red carpet with splurge-worthy food and kitchen gifts, look no further.

The casual gift for someone who loves food and loves to host might be nice set of chip and dip bowls, cocktail napkins, or perhaps some beeswax candlesticks. The gift of a whole dry-cured Spanish ham leg, however, is a next-level present for the most passionate entertainer in your family or friend group.

No better way to pull focus at the dining table than with this copper and brass pepper mill, which East Fork says can literally last for “hundreds of years” when cared for properly. The 10-inch tall grinder is made in collaboration with a small, family-run company in Greece, and is actually modeled after the same mills 20th-century Greek soldiers would carry to grind coffee, a fact that finds homage in the Greek lettering inscribed on the mill.

The Eater staff has tested its fare share of toaster ovens, and crowned the Balmuda as one of the best for its minimalist design and ability to not just warm but rehydrate breads and pastries; it uses a steam process to reinvigorate that day-old croissant like a wizard. This Balmuda Pro has an even more powerful heat source, and a setting called Salamander Grill Mode for giving your salmon the restaurant-grade finishing treatment.

The cultural martini discourse has never been stronger, or brinier. Help your giftee celebrate Hanukkah with Susan Alexandra’s dirty martini menorah. As the designer’s site proclaims, “The miracle of Hanukkah was that the olive oil that was enough only for one day of light lasted for eight days. Our favorite way of consuming olives? In a bath of vodka/ gin and a touch of vermouth!”

Behold, a splurge that is also a cooking investment! We’ve all experienced the frustration of chopping special ingredients on a sub-par cutting board, and the moment you level up to a thick, handsome slab is one that can help give you newfound confidence and efficiency as a passionate home cook. Boardsmith’s walnut end grain cutting boards are all made to order out of a sustainably harvested black walnut, resulting in beautiful, checkerboard-like and ombré color variations. Cheese boards have never looked better, folks.

The Chicago-based luxury chocolatier Vosges is known for its intricate, decadent holiday gifts (don’t miss its lodge-inspired advent calendar), and it has curated the perfect assortment of its truffles to go with a bottle of Ceretto Barolo wine. “This is a classic Barolo,” the site explains, “[it’s] light garnet in color with Barolo’s quintessential aromas of roses, tart cherries, and hints of truffles.”

Made in Victor, Idaho, the boutique blades of New West KniveWorks are a departure from the recent fad of making knives extra wide, favoring instead the graceful docility of a light, 8-inch steel blade and a handle made out of a durable resin composite material that will last a lifetime. In the fighting words of New West, “this precision instrument isn’t a club like Mom’s old Wüsthof Trident.” If you’re shopping for a partner who tends to their knife collection like the Crown Jewels, it’s the kind of gift that feels equal parts lifetime cooking investment and personality-forward essential tool.

Gohar World’s elevated kitchen essentials walk the line between Dalí-esque absurdity (remember when Julia Fox wore its kitchen gloves to the Grammys?) and functionality, and this metallic apron is no exception: it lends you a lacy hand (two, actually) while you’re cooking.

I really do think the Moccamaster coffee machine is the Platonic ideal of drip coffee machines; my own yellow pepper model swept me off my feet with its talent for quick, smooth brewing and its modular, chic mid-century modern design. If you love someone who loves coffee — and perhaps already owns the GOATed machine — why not invest in the brand’s powerful burr grinder? It’s certified by the European Coffee Brewing Centre (ECBC), which means it has passed a rigorous testing process for uniform grinding and quality construction.

Imagine casually inviting your beloved over for dinner, and you serve this gorgeous Japanese wagyu ribeye steak along with an Old-Fashioned? Imperia Caviar is best known for its royal osetra, but it’s also where you can find a variety of A5 Japanese wagyu (the highest designation for beef in the country); this grade of wagyu has up to five times more intramuscular fat, which makes for an even richer, buttery flavor.

I always have a few lighters floating around my house for candles and incense, but there’s something so retro-chic about a coffee table lighter. Edie Parker, master of eccentric and surreal lifestyle [puffs chamomile pre-roll] accessories has a line of jelly-inspired tabletop lighters with all kinds of “fillings,” and the olive version is one of the most charming.

Unsurprisingly, we’re picky when it comes to choosing cookware at Eater — that’s why we collaborated with Heritage Steel to make the kind of cookware collection that will last a lifetime. Every frypan, lid, and pot is made out of 5-ply stainless steel, and this robust bundle includes everything you need to embark on all kinds of culinary adventures: two fry pans (8.5- and 10.5-inch), a 2-quart saucier, a 3-quart saucepan, a 4-quart sauté pan, and an 8-quart stock pot ready to simmer your most Strega Nona-worthy stews.

Here’s an idea: Order this massive wheel of Manchego cheese from Flamingo Estate, and ride it to victory at the Cooper’s Hill cheese rolling competition. That, or gift it to someone who can appreciate the fact that it’s sourced, per Flamingo Estate, from one of only ten cheese mongers in Spain that are still making farmstead PDO Manchego Artesano, which results in an even richer and more complex flavor.

You know the big (or rather, full-size) Rocco: a $1,500 high-tech drink fridge, endorsed by Eric Wareheim and seemingly designed by someone who loves Eames chairs. This year, Rocco has launched a miniature version of its posh drink refrigerator, dubbed the Mini Mini Fridge, this 14-inch tall personal fridge fits up to 12 cans of your preferred beverages (or sheet masks; choose your journey). Unlike most mini fridges, the Mini cools down to 39 degrees Fahrenheit (the majority of countertop fridges hit 48 degrees Fahrenheit at their coldest). Kind of the dream set up for your — sorry, your giftee’s — office.

Atelier Sebastião Lobo crafts otherworldly flatware that’s almost too beautiful to use. This set of Calder-esque cutlery has spawned many imitations, because it’s one of the most original designs to come out of the flatware world in recent years, and a prime example of how cutlery and tableware in general got really squiggly and freaky this year.

There is nothing like devoting counter space to yet another coffee machine that requires highly specific capsules, but hey! This one is different — it brews only cold coffee. (Nitro cold brew, cold brew, and cold espresso to be specific.) Sure, it’s definitely a bit of a luxury, but then again, so is spending $7 on an iced cortado from the coffee shop every morning.

N/A drinks were created to be a more inclusive product. Only a rare few can order bottles of bubbly for over $100. The Venn diagram where these two groups overlap is small, but it exists, along with this $119 bottle of booze-free bubbly made with French Chardonnay grapes.

In a way that I cannot quite explain, this feels like it’s targeted at the 1990s kids who grew up with Smart House and Richie Rich. This stationary exercise bike, complete with an orange slice wheel, whips up one of your favorite smoothies courtesy of your own pedaling power. As one reviewer writes, “I am 67 years old, widowed twice, and I have seen enough in this life to know when somebody has finally invented something useful. This bicycle-blender contraption has changed the direction of my spirit. Every morning I put in one banana, some frozen peaches, yogurt, a little honey, and whatever green thing is closest to expiration in my refrigerator. Then I pedal until either the smoothie is done or I start seeing little sparkles. Whichever comes first.”

Khushbu Shah is the former restaurant editor at Food & Wine and the author of the cookbook AMRIKAN: 125 Recipes From the Indian American Diaspora. She lives in Los Angeles and you can follow all of her egg eating adventures on Instagram.

#6270. AI Helps Three Powerful Supercomputers Simulate The Milky Way In Extraordinary Detail

In the early days, astronomers kept sketchbooks close at hand when they looked through their telescopes. They drew what they saw and shared their drawings. Modern astronomy, with its enormous segmented lenses, gigabyte cameras, and cryogenically-cooled infrared space observatories, makes those days seem more distant than they really are. But one of the latest efforts in astronomy makes astronomy's sketch-pad days seem so far in the past, they're almost red-shifted.

In an impressive technological maneuver, astronomers have harnessed three different supercomputers together to simulate the Milky Way at a level of detail never before achieved. They used the supercomputers and AI together to simulate the Milky Way down to the level of individual stars. Up until now, the smallest level of detail in simulations, called particles, was clusters of stars with the mass of about 100 Suns. The behaviour of individual stars was averaged out in those simulations (Auriga, FIRE, etc.)

These results are in a paper titled "Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy," from the SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis. The lead author is Keiya Hirashima, from RIKEN in Japan.

In simulations, achieving a level of individual stars means that individually simulated particles have one solar mass. So it's like a proxy for the population of stars. But regardless of that important distinction, the new simulations are extraordinary.

"Our highest-resolution Milky Way simulation used 5.4 trillion particles, â¼ 10, 000Ã those in the state-of-the-art simulations," the authors write.

âWe expect better simulations as computational power increases, but this still requires work on improving resolutions, and for a Milky Way-sized galaxy, itâs not straightforward,â said Professor Michiko Fujii from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Tokyo. âWhen we look at smaller regions in detail, we encounter areas where the gas is denser and changes rapidly. This means the simulation needs to take much shorter steps in time, which greatly increases the amount of calculation required."

This figure from the paper shows different structures of disk galaxies at different scales, emphasizing the complexity necessary for accurate simulations. Top left and middle: NGC 4414, a disk galaxy similar to the Milky Way Galaxy, taken with the Hubble Space Telescope. Top right: NGC628, a disk galaxy with spiral arms and bubble structures taken with the JWST. Bottom left: Carina star forming region taken with the JWST. Bottom middle: Cassiopeia A supernova remnant taken with the JWST. Bottom right: turbulent innterstellar gas around Cassiopeia A taken with Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. Image Credit: Hirashima et al. 2026. SC2026.

To achieve this fine particle resolution, simulations need ever shorter time steps, and time steps are like simulation currency; the shorter they are, the more computing resources they demand. To supply the resources for that, the researchers harnessed the power of three exascale supercomputers together: Aurora, Frontier, and JUPITER. Each one ran the same software on different hardware: Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD graphic processing units (GPUs) and central processing units (CPUs).

But linking three supercomputers was only part of the solution.

"We overcame this problem by using an AI model to predict how gas around supernova explosions evolves," said Fujii. "This allowed us to carry out the simulation more efficiently and achieve a level of detail where individual stars can be represented."

By using this model, the larger simulation was able to skip over many small timesteps. It's called PHEASANT, and it was developed by postdoctoral researcher Keiya Hirashima from RIKEN. Supernovae are complex and require their own detailed simulations with very small timesteps. By plugging PHEASANT into the larger simulation, it relieved that simulation of a lot of work.

"With trillions of particles, we resolve individual stars and model their SN feedback self-consistently within a galactic-scale simulation," the authors write. "Such a simulation reveals how individual stars, such as the Sun, contribute to the overall structure of the MW through multiple physical processes."

This image from PHEASANT shows the Milky Way's disk. Galaxies are complex structures, with different types of structures at different scales. They have thin and thick disks, bulges, halos, spiral arms, star clusters, nebulae, and individual stars and gas clouds. In this work, the researchers divided the galaxy into smaller regions that could be processed by different parts of a supercomputer. Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND

âOne of my parts was to develop an AI model that predicts how the gas surrounding a supernova explosion changes over time. If we calculate this process directly, we need time steps of around 100 years,â said Hirashima. âMy model predicts gas distribution after 100,000 years. This means that, rather than having to calculate every small step, we can use a much longer time step for the entire galaxy simulation. Making this work efficiently on different supercomputers was a challenge because each system uses different AMD, Intel, or NVIDIA CPUs and GPUs. Achieving good performance across all three systems required some specific optimizations.â

These panels are snapshots from PHEASANT. The panel on the left shows the distribution and temperature of gas across a model galaxy. The panel on the right is a close-up view, where individual stars are visible as dots. Image Credit: Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND

We can't understand the Milky Way, or galaxies in general, without a detailed understanding of how its gas and stars behave. Stars are born, drift away from their clusters, and evolve. Depending on their masses, they can remain on the main sequence for trillions of years, leave the main sequence after a few billion years and then linger as white dwarf cinders, or exhaust their fuel rapidly and explode as supernovae.

Gas is also complex. It collects in clouds where stars form, can be funnelled into the galactic center and "recycled" by supermassive black holes, or blasted away by explosions. Stars and gas are linked, and there's an extraordinary amount of detail involved.

Supernovae are among the most complicated events. In some regions, the massive young stars that eventually explode as supernova are born in the same region. When they exhaust their fuel, they explode and carve massive bubbles in the interstellar medium. That can drive gas away to form more new stars elsewhere. They can even propel gas outside of the galaxy. It's all part of the life of the Milky Way, and simulations that struggle to recreate all of the detail in supernova explosions can lead astronomers astray.

This is LHA 120-N44 (N44) in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the ESO's Very Large Telescope. It features a massive bubble excavated in the interstellar medium by exploding young stars in its center. Some of the stars are still there, and they're still expanding the bubble with their powerful winds. Simulating all of the complexity involved is an enormous challenge. Image Credit: ESO/Manu Mejias

âSomething we want to understand is how events on the scale of individual stars connect to the larger structure of the Milky Way,â said Fujii. âWith this simulation, we can investigate how individual supernovae affect the number of stars that form, the size of these giant gas bubbles and the material that flows out of the galaxy. We can also study how groups of stars form and how they may eventually develop into star clusters.â

The PHEASANT AI surrogate model plays a critical role in this work, and that's part of a broader trend in science.

"The surrogate modeling approach can also be generalized beyond astrophysical problems to other research fields," the authors write.

"AI surrogate modeling accelerates simulations and bridges wider physical scales, opening new pathways in various real-world applications, including climate modeling, space forecasting, and low-temperature plasma," the authors conclude.

#6269. An Overlooked Metabolic Byproduct Could Help Repair a Damaged Heart

A substance often treated as waste may be vital to the heart during a crisis, offering a potential target for treating heart failure and heart attacks.

The heart has to keep beating whether the body has plenty of energy available or is running low. Maintaining that constant supply of energy is a complicated process, and when it breaks down, it can contribute to serious cardiovascular conditions such as heart failure. Researchers at University of Utah Health have now uncovered an unusual feature of heart muscle cells that helps them stay fueled during periods of stress and could point toward new ways to treat a damaged heart.

Scientists previously knew that the heart could draw energy from two carbohydrate sources at once: glucose, a sugar, and lactate, a substance produced when cells break down glucose. In most human tissues, increasing the use of one fuel makes it harder to use the other. Heart muscle somehow avoids this competition.

In a study published in Nature, researchers discovered that heart muscle cells process these fuels in separate parts of the cell. Glucose is broken down in the cytosol, the fluid that surrounds structures inside the cell, while lactate is used inside mitochondria, which produce much of the cell’s usable energy. Keeping these processes separate allows the heart to draw energy from both sources simultaneously.

The system depends on a molecule called MCT1, which transports lactate into the mitochondria. The researchers found that genetic mutations affecting MCT1 prevented lactate from entering the mitochondria and disrupted the heart’s energy balance. Although the heart could largely function without this pathway under everyday conditions, losing it when the heart was under stress led to heart failure.

“This appears to be a critical backup system for heart function,” says Gregory Ducker, PhD, assistant professor of biochemistry at University of Utah Health and senior author of the study. “In an emergency, we would really, really rely on this.”

The discovery identifies a previously unrecognized role for lactate in sustaining injured heart muscle and gives researchers a potential target for developing treatments that restore its energy supply.

“Our findings help point to new areas in which we could target the heart muscle to benefit and repair itself by allowing it to use lactate better,” Ducker says. “That’s the long-term goal: to help the heart muscle heal.”

Whether enhancing this energy pathway can improve heart function in patients remains to be established, though the researchers see potential applications beyond heart failure.

“Rather than simply releasing lactate into the bloodstream as a waste product, we may be able to enhance the heart’s ability to use it as a valuable source of energy,” says Stavros Drakos, MD, PhD, professor of medicine at University of Utah Health and co-senior author of the study. “By optimizing this process, we could potentially improve heart muscle function in patients suffering from heart failure or heart attacks.”

Reference: “MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism” by Ahmad A. Cluntun, Joseph R. Visker, Jesse N. Velasco-Silva, James Carrington, Luis Cedeño-Rosario, Giulia C. Napoli, Ji Eon Kim, Thirupura S. Shankar, Marisa J. Brothwell, Rana Hamouche, Álvaro J. Narbona-Pérez, Jing Ling, Ashish G. Toshniwal, Hayden K. Low, Corey N. Cunningham, David R. Eberhardt, Jing Li, Claire E. Stanley, Queren A. Alcantara, Tarun Yadav, Ryan L. Maves, Wojciech I. Swiatek, Nicholas A. Offei, Bhavya Blaze, Sumangala P. Shetty, Dipayan Chaudhuri, Tingting Hong, Jeffery D. Rothstein, Deborah M. Muoio, Joao A. Paulo, Steven P. Gygi, Eleni Tseliou, Sutip Navankasattusas, James E. Cox, Katsuhiko Funai, Stavros G. Drakos, Jared Rutter and Gregory S. Ducker, 28 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11182-3
